title: Zones and junk defenses
text:
Guarding areas instead of players, and hybrids built to erase one scorer.
All families · 10 terms · 9 full, 0 partial, 1 short

1-2-2 zone
One defender at the top, two at the elbows, two on the blocks; it covers the arc better than a 2-3 and the baseline worse.

Why it is run. One at the top and two at the elbows covers the arc better than a 2-3, and two on the blocks covers the baseline better than a 3-2, at the cost of doing neither as well as the shape built for it.
What beats it. The quick wing-to-corner pass before the elbow defender steps out; the same high-post and short-corner attacks that beat the 2-3.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also 2-3 zone, 3-2 zone


1-3-1 zone
One at the top, three across the free-throw line, one on the baseline; built to trap and force long passes.

Why it is run. A long thin shape with a point and a baseline runner exists to trap the wing catch with two defenders and force the long pass out of it; it is a gamble on turnovers, not a scheme of protection.
What beats it. The skip pass out of the trap to the far corner, which the single runner cannot reach; a handler who keeps his dribble and splits the trap.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense


2-3 zone
Two defenders up top and three across the baseline, packing the paint.

Why it is run. Two up and three across the back closes the paint completely and keeps the rim protector at the rim; it is thin at the high post, where the two lines meet, and in the corners the back line has to stretch to.
What beats it. The high-post entry and the pass from there to the corner; the skip pass when the whole zone has shifted; offensive rebounds against a back line with nobody to box out.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense, 3-2 zone


3-2 zone
Three across the free-throw line extended and two on the blocks, pressuring shooters at the cost of the glass.

Why it is run. Three across the free-throw line extended crowds the arc against a shooting team and guards the high post; two players are left with the whole baseline and the glass.
What beats it. The short-corner catch behind the low pair; the drive into the gap between a top defender and a low one; the offensive rebound.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense


Box-and-one
Four defenders in a box zone with one chasing the opponent’s best player man-to-man.

Why it is run. Against a team with one scorer and little around him, one defender in the scorer’s chest all game and a four-man box behind him bets that the other four attackers cannot beat a zone.
What beats it. The other four attackers scoring; the chased scorer setting screens, which the box has no rule for; a big posting against a zone that has no one to double.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense, Junk defense


Diamond-and-one
The box-and-one with the four zone defenders in a diamond, one at the top, one on each side of the lane and one under the rim, while the fifth chases the scorer.

Why it is run. Turning the box forty-five degrees puts a zone defender at the free-throw line and one in front of the rim, so the top of the key and the rim are guarded better than the box guards them, and the blocks and short corners worse.
What beats it. The unchased attackers scoring from the blocks and short corners the diamond leaves thin; the chased scorer setting screens, which the zone has no rule for.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Box-and-one, Junk defense


Junk defense
Also: combination defense
Any zone-and-man hybrid built to take one player out of a game.

defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Box-and-one


Match-up zone
A zone whose defenders take the player in their area man-to-man while he is there.

Why it is run. A zone shape with man principles inside it shows the offense a defender on every catch and a zone on every pass, so neither its zone offense nor its man offense finds what it was built for.
What beats it. Cutters through the seams faster than the hand-off can be made; the overload that puts two attackers in one area.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense, Man-to-man


Triangle-and-two
Two defenders chase the opponent’s two best players man-to-man while the other three form a triangle zone, one at the free-throw line and two on the blocks.

Why it is run. Two chasers on the two scorers and a three-man triangle behind them concedes the arc to the other three attackers entirely, which is only a bet worth making when the defense is sure they cannot make it.
What beats it. The three unchased attackers shooting; the two scorers screening for each other and dragging the chasers into the triangle.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Box-and-one, Junk defense


Zone defense
Each defender guards an area rather than a player.

Why it is run. Guarding areas instead of men puts more bodies in the paint than man-to-man can, removes the ball screen as a problem, and hides a slow big in the middle; the arc, the skip pass and the glass are the price.
What beats it. Zone offense: the high-post catch where two areas meet, the short corner behind the back line, the overload, and the skip pass to the side the zone has just left.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also 2-3 zone, Match-up zone, Man-to-man

title: Transition defense
text:
Rim, ball, then match up. In that order.
All families · 13 terms · 11 full, 2 partial, 0 short

Crash or get back
The trade-off, decided per team and per shot, between sending players to the offensive glass and sending them back on defense.
Why it is run. Offensive rebounds are worth a lot; giving up run-outs costs a lot. There is no free answer; a team picks a rule and the rule depends on who is on the floor.
offense / defense · Transition · partial · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Floor balance, Leak out


Cross-match
A deliberate transition match-up that is not the half-court assignment, such as a wing taking the opposing big so the big can run to the rim.
Why it is run. The defensive big is often the last man back. Letting the nearest wing take the offensive big, and the big take the wing, keeps the rim protected.
What beats it. The offense attacking the size mismatch before the defense can swap back.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Match up, Scram switch


Floor balance
Also: safety, get-back man
The offensive team’s rule for who stays back on a shot so the other team cannot run.
Why it is run. Every offensive rebounder is one fewer player getting back. Most teams designate one or two players who retreat as the shot goes up.
What beats it. The offense crashing everyone and betting the extra possessions outweigh the run-outs.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Crash or get back, Leak out


Jam the rebounder
Also: pressure the outlet
Pressuring the defensive rebounder as he lands, and denying the outlet man, so the break starts late.
Why it is run. A break that starts one second late is a break that meets a set defense. The player nearest the rebounder stays on him instead of turning to run.
What beats it. A rebounder who outlets on the way down, and a second outlet option.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Outlet pass, Stop the ball


Load to the ball
Retreating defenders shading toward the side the ball is on, so the ball-handler sees bodies and the far side is left for last.
Why it is run. The ball scores; the far-side player has to be passed to first. Loading to the ball takes away the drive and dares the long skip pass.
What beats it. The skip pass to the weak-side corner.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Stop the ball


Match up
Also: find a body, find your man
The last job getting back: each defender taking a player, not necessarily his own, so every attacker is guarded.
Why it is run. In transition there is no time to find your assignment. The rule is to take the nearest unguarded attacker and sort out the mismatches after the possession is under control.
What beats it. The offense hunting the mismatch that the emergency match-up created.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Transition defense, Cross-match, Scram switch


No layups
Also: make them shoot over you
The transition rule that the paint is protected before anything else, so the shot conceded is a jumper, never a layup.
Why it is run. A rule a tired player can follow. When a defender does not know where to go, he goes to the paint.
What beats it. The transition three.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Transition three


Pick-up point
How far up the floor the defense meets the ball; at the free-throw line extended, at half court, or full court.
Why it is run. A higher pick-up slows the offense earlier but costs the defender ground behind him. Teams pick it by their personnel and by how much they trust their rim protection.
defense · Transition · partial · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Stop the ball, Press


Protect the rim first
Also: build the wall, paint first
The first job getting back: the first defenders sprint to the paint, not to a man, and then close out from there.

Why it is run. A layup is the shot transition gives up most and costs most. Sprinting to the paint takes it away; everything else is closed out to from the inside.
What beats it. The corner fill and the transition three, which are the shots the offense takes when the paint is closed.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Transition defense, Stop the ball, Corner fill


Stop the ball
Also: pick up the ball, pick-up point
One defender meeting the ball-handler early to slow the dribble and turn the break into a half-court possession.
Why it is run. A ball-handler at full speed beats a defender back-pedalling. Met early, he has to slow down, and the defense behind him gets the seconds it needs.
What beats it. The hit-ahead pass, which moves the ball past the pick-up point without dribbling into it.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Pick-up point, Hit-ahead pass


Tandem defense
Also: I formation, two-on-one defense
Two defenders against three attackers lined up one in front of the other: the front man takes the ball, the back man takes the first pass, then they rotate.

Why it is run. Side by side, two defenders leave the middle open. In a line, the ball is met at the free-throw line and the rim is still protected; the first pass is taken by the back man and the front man drops to the rim.
What beats it. Swinging the ball twice fast, or a shooter stopping for the three instead of running to the rim.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Numbers advantage, Protect the rim first


Transition defense
Also: getting back
Everything the defense does between losing the ball and being set in the half court.
Why it is run. The offense is trying to score before the defense is organized. The defense’s job, in order, is to protect the rim, stop the ball, and then match up.
What beats it. The push and the hit-ahead, which try to beat the defense to those three jobs.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Stop the ball, Match up, Floor balance


Transition take foul
Also: take foul, Euro foul
A deliberate foul on the ball early in a break to stop the play before the numbers advantage can be used.
Why it is run. Trading two free throws for a near-certain layup was, for years, worth it. It is worth less than it was.
What beats it. None on the floor; the counter came from the rule book.
What changed. From the 2022-23 season the NBA penalizes a transition take foul with one free throw, shot by any player on the offended team, plus possession, so the foul no longer trades the break for two free throws.

Source: registry nba-2022-take-foul. NBA.com, dated July 13, 2022. Verbatim: “Beginning with the 2022-23 NBA season”, then two bullets: “The offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “The offensive team will retain possession of the ball.” A first URL remembered for this entry returned 404 and was replaced; the entry was not published on the remembered one. Converted from an inline url/title/retrieved source to this registry row on 2026-09-21 (Phase 3a); the saved text is data/sources/nba-2022-take-foul.txt.

defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Transition defense, Stop the ball

title: Sets and systems
text:
Alignments, called plays, and the rule-based offenses that run without a call.
All families · 14 terms · 12 full, 1 partial, 1 short

4-on-3
The advantage behind a trap: four attackers against the three defenders who did not trap.

Why it is run. Two defenders on the ball leaves three to guard four; the weak-side low man cannot cover the dunker spot and the corner at once, and the pass out of the trap goes to whichever he leaves.
What beats it. Rotations quick enough to cover four spots with three men until the trap recovers, and a trap timed so the shot clock does the rest.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Blitz, Short roll


Delay
Also: 5-out delay
An early-offense alignment with the big at the top holding the ball and the four others spaced, from which he hands off, screens or reverses.

Why it is run. With the big holding the ball at the arc and nobody in the paint, his defender must choose between guarding him twenty-five feet out and protecting a rim nobody is near; either choice opens the handoff or the drive.
What beats it. The big’s defender guarding him at the arc and denying the handoff, or the defense switching every handoff so no cutter gets the ball moving.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also 5-out, Dribble handoff, Zoom


Dribble drive motion
Also: DDM, dribble drive
A spread offense with no post player in the lane, built on driving gaps and kicking out or dropping off when the help comes.

Why it is run. With the lane empty and the big in the weak-side dunker spot, a drive into a double gap forces one help defender to choose between the rim and the corner, and the pass goes to whoever he left.
What beats it. Guarding the drive with one man and never helping, which needs defenders who stay in front, or walling off the middle and conceding the pull-up.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.9 · See also 5-out, Drive, Kick-out, Gap


Flex offense
Also: flex cut
A continuity offense whose repeating unit is a baseline cross screen followed by a down screen for the screener.

Why it is run. A cross screen and a down screen for the screener return the floor to its own starting shape, so the sequence can run again until one defender is late.
What beats it. Switching both screens, which is available to a team of similar-sized players, or going under the cross screen every time and living with the seal.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.9 · See also Cross screen, Pin-down, Ram


Flow offense
Offense that runs continuously from transition into half-court actions without a called play, governed by rules for who screens and who spaces.
offense · Early offense · short · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Early offense, Motion offense


Horns
An alignment with two bigs at the elbows, two shooters in the corners and the ball at the top.

Why it is run. Two bigs at the elbows and two shooters in the corners empties the paint, puts two screeners one pass from the ball, and makes several different plays look identical for the first two seconds.
What beats it. Switching everything, which removes the screens and concedes the mismatches, or a big at the level of the ball screen with the low man tagging the roller.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.8 · See also Elbow, Pick-and-roll


Isolation
Also: iso
Clearing a side so one player can attack one defender.

Why it is run. When one attacker beats one defender by himself, the best use of the other four is to stand where their defenders cannot help.
What beats it. A defender who stays in front; or sending a second defender early and living with the pass out.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Mismatch, Switch


Mismatch
A matchup the offense can exploit, such as a big guarding a guard on the perimeter or a guard guarding a big in the post.

Why it is run. A switch leaves a big on a guard or a guard on a big, and both halves are attackable: the guard drives the slower man, the big posts the smaller one.
What beats it. The scram switch, switching back at the first dead ball, or a roster similar enough in size that no switch creates one.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Switch, Isolation, Early seal


Motion offense
Offense run from rules rather than a script, where players read the defense and cut or screen accordingly.

Why it is run. Rules attached to the pass produce screening and cutting continuously, so the defense must guard correctly every time, and the offense needs no call and can be run at any tempo.
What beats it. Switching everything, which turns every screen into a non-event and dares the offense to win one-on-one; or physical denial of the first pass.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Flow offense, Set play, Read and react


Pistol
Also: 21, Nash action
An early-offense entry where the guard passes ahead to the wing and follows the pass into a handoff or a quick ball screen.

Why it is run. Passing ahead and following the pass turns the best ball-handler’s defender’s one relaxed step into a handoff taken at speed toward the middle, with a big’s screen already coming.
What beats it. Switching the handoff, or top-locking the guard so he cannot follow his pass.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Dribble handoff, Early offense


Princeton offense
A read-based offense built on a high-post entry, back cuts against overplay, and screens away from the ball.

Why it is run. The high post passes and every denial becomes a back cut, so a defense that presses the perimeter gives up layups and a defense that sags gives up the catch.
What beats it. Refusing to deny: play a step off, concede the perimeter catch and take away the cuts, so the offense has to shoot over a set defense.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.9 · See also Back cut, Motion offense, Read and react


Read and react
A conceptual offense where every off-ball player has a rule for each thing the ball does.

Why it is run. Every player has a reaction to the drive, executed before the drive resolves, so the three outlets are already moving when the help commits.
What beats it. A defense that never helps, so no reaction is triggered; or shrinking the floor so every drive is into a single gap.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Motion offense, 45 cut, Lift


Set play
A scripted sequence run to get a particular shot for a particular player.
Why it is run. Five players know what is coming and the defense does not; the cost is three or four seconds of setup during which the defense gets organized, which is why teams run them after timeouts, for a specific player, and at the end of a period.
offense · Half court · partial · Taught in lecture 3.8 · See also Motion offense, ATO


Zipper
A player cutting from the block straight up the lane line off a down screen to catch at the top.

Why it is run. A cut straight up the lane line off a screen delivers the catch at the slot with the whole floor in front of the catcher, and usually straight into a ball screen from the man who just screened.
What beats it. Top-locking the cutter so he cannot come up the lane line, conceding the back cut, or switching the screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.8 · See also Pin-down

title: Rules: NCAA women
text:
Edition on file: 2025-26 and 2026-27 Women’s Rules Book, online version updated 1 September 2026.
Text status: on-file.
Document: NCAA Women’s Basketball Rules Book, retrieved 2026-09-21.
The full rules book PDF, extracted with pypdf: 51,092 words, with the same period extraction quirk as the men’s book. The restricted-area arc appears only on the court diagram (an image, page 20 in the book’s own index), so its radius is a gap here even though the book is on file.
All five compared · NBA · NCAA men · FIBA · NFHS (US high school).

title: Rules: NCAA women
text:
The floor and spacing

Restricted area
The half-circle in front of the rim inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge. Entry.
No arc. The restricted area is the floor directly under the basket, from the front and side of the ring to the front of the backboard; the book recommends removing any painted arc. Rule 1-8.1

Verbatim: “The restricted area is that area of the playing court located directly underneath each basket” and “is defined as from the front and side of the ring to the front of the backboard” and, in the book’s note, “It is recommended that the three-foot arc, or four-foot arc on courts used only by women’s basketball programs, be removed the next time the playing court is refinished.”

title: Rules: NCAA women
text:
Transition defense

Transition take foul
A deliberate foul on the ball early in a break to stop the play before the numbers advantage can be used. Entry.
No transition-specific foul; contact designed to negate an opponent’s obvious advantageous position is a flagrant 1 foul. Rule 10-13.1.b

Verbatim: “A flagrant 1 foul is a player-contact foul which, in the judgment of the official, is:” then “Contact designed to negate an opponent’s obvious advantageous position”. The text was also searched for the phrases take foul, transition, fast break and clear path; none names a rule.

title: Rules: NCAA women
text:
Rules and regulations

Backcourt count
The time a team has to bring the ball across the midcourt line; the count a press is built to run out. Entry.
10 seconds. Rule 9-10

Verbatim: “shall not be in continuous control of a ball that is in their backcourt for 10 consecutive seconds”.



Court dimensions
The length and width of the playing court. Entry.
94 feet by 50 feet, inside the boundary lines. Rule 1-2.2

Verbatim: “The playing court shall be a rectangular surface free from obstructions with sidelines of 94 feet in length and end lines of 50 feet in length, measured from the inside edges of these lines”.



Defensive three seconds
The NBA rule that a defender in the lane must be guarding someone within three seconds; the reason a rim protector cannot simply stand under the basket. Entry.
No such rule; checked against NCAA Women’s Basketball Rules Book.

The book’s three-second rule restricts the offensive player only; its text was searched for a defensive count and none appears. The offensive rule reads, verbatim: “it is a violation when a player exceeds three seconds in the lane and there is no try for goal”.



Free-throw lane
How wide the painted lane is; the number behind the paint, the blocks and the elbows. Entry.
12 feet, measured to the outside of the lane lines. Rule 1-6.1

Verbatim: “A free-throw lane, 12 feet wide measured to the outside of each lane boundary”.



Free-throw line
How far the free-throw line is from the backboard; it fixes the nail and the elbows. Entry.
15 feet from the plane of the face of the backboard. Rule 1-6

Verbatim: “It shall be parallel to the end line and shall have its farthest edge 15 feet from the plane of the face of the backboard”.



Goaltending
Touching a shot on its way down, or off the backboard, while it can still score; the rule that limits what a rim protector may do. Entry.
A violation, alongside basket interference; only the defensive team’s goaltending awards points. Rule 9-15.1; Rule 5-1.18

Verbatim: “It is a violation to commit basket interference or goaltending” and “The only infractions for which points are awarded are goaltending or basket interference by the defensive team”.



Length of the game
How long a game is and how it is divided; the one rule every other clock hangs on. Entry.
Four quarters of 10 minutes. Rule 5-6.1

Verbatim: “Playing time for varsity games shall consist of four 10-minute quarters with a halftime intermission of 15 minutes”.



Shot clock
The time a team has to attempt a shot that reaches the ring; the number that sets the pace of every possession. Entry.
30 seconds; reset to 20 on a frontcourt throw-in after a dead-ball change of team control. Rule 2-11.1; Rule 2-11.6.d

Verbatim: “Use a 30-second shot clock” and, from the summary of changes, “The shot clock will be set to 20 seconds when, following a dead-ball change of team control, a team is awarded the ball for a throw-in in their frontcourt”.



Three-point line
How far the arc is from the basket, and how far the corner line is from the sideline; the geometry every spacing decision in Chapter 3 rests on. Entry.
22 feet 1¾ inches from the center of the basket; 21 feet 7⅞ inches in the corners. Rule 1-7.1

Verbatim: “The three-point field-goal line shall be a distance of 22 feet, 13/4 inches from the center of the basket to the outside edge of the three-point field-goal line and 21 feet, 77/8 inches in the corners”.

title: Rules: NBA
text:
Edition on file: Official Rules as published per rule at official.nba.com; rules 1, 5, 7, 10, 11 and 12 retrieved 2026-09-17 to 2026-09-21.
Text status: on-file.
Document: RULE NO. 1: Court Dimensions - Equipment, retrieved 2026-09-21.
The NBA publishes its rulebook one rule per web page. Six of the rule pages are on file (1, 5, 7, 10, 11, 12), each as its own registry row; a cell cites the page it comes from. Rule No. 1’s text defers the court’s overall dimensions and the lane width to a diagram it does not print, so those two cells are gaps at the NBA even though the text is on file. The transition take foul is cited to the league’s 2022 announcement of the change, because the Rule 12 page on file does not carry the words.
All five compared · NCAA men · NCAA women · FIBA · NFHS (US high school).

title: Rules: NBA
text:
The floor and spacing

Restricted area
The half-circle in front of the rim inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge. Entry.
A half-circle 4 feet from the center of the basket ring, extended parallel to the lane line to the face of the backboard. Rule No. 1, Section I

Verbatim, in the page’s own characters: “A Restricted Area shall be marked with a half-circle 4’ from the center of the basket ring and then parallel to the lane line to the face of the backboard with a solid two-inch line.”

title: Rules: NBA
text:
Transition defense

Transition take foul
A deliberate foul on the ball early in a break to stop the play before the numbers advantage can be used. Entry.
From 2022-23, one free throw by any player on the offended team, and the offended team keeps the ball. Board of Governors announcement, 13 July 2022 (the Rule 12 page on file does not carry the words; no rule number is printed in the release)

Verbatim: “The offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “The offensive team will retain possession of the ball.”

title: Rules: NBA
text:
Rules and regulations

Backcourt count
The time a team has to bring the ball across the midcourt line; the count a press is built to run out. Entry.
8 seconds. Rule No. 10, Section VIII

Verbatim: “A team shall not be in continuous possession of a ball which is in its backcourt for more than 8 consecutive seconds.”



Court dimensions
The length and width of the playing court. Entry.
Gap: not in the public text of NBA; searched RULE NO. 1: Court Dimensions - Equipment.

Rule No. 1 defers to a diagram it does not print: “The playing court shall be measured and marked as shown in the court (See below)”. The 94 by 50 feet this site draws is taken from a secondary source and marked as such in tools/court.py.



Defensive three seconds
The NBA rule that a defender in the lane must be guarding someone within three seconds; the reason a rim protector cannot simply stand under the basket. Entry.
A defender in the 16-foot lane, or within 4 feet beyond its endline, must be actively guarding an opponent within three seconds while the offense controls the ball in the frontcourt. Rule No. 10, Section VII

Verbatim: “Any defensive player, who is positioned in the 16-foot lane or the area extending 4 feet past the lane endline, must be actively guarding an opponent within three seconds.” and “Actively guarding means being within arm’s length of an offensive player and in a guarding position.”



Free-throw lane
How wide the painted lane is; the number behind the paint, the blocks and the elbows. Entry.
16 feet. Rule No. 10, Section VII

Rule No. 1 defers the lane to a diagram it does not print, so the width is taken from the defensive three-second rule, verbatim: “Any defensive player, who is positioned in the 16-foot lane or the area extending 4 feet past the lane endline, must be actively guarding an opponent within three seconds.”



Free-throw line
How far the free-throw line is from the backboard; it fixes the nail and the elbows. Entry.
15 feet from the plane of the face of the backboard. Rule No. 1, Section I

Verbatim, in the page’s own characters: “It shall be parallel to the end line and shall be 15’ from the plane of the face of the backboard.”



Goaltending
Touching a shot on its way down, or off the backboard, while it can still score; the rule that limits what a rim protector may do. Entry.
A player may not touch a ball on its downward flight with a chance to score, nor a ball that has touched the backboard above ring level, nor a ball within the cylinder above the ring. Rule No. 11, Section I

Verbatim: “Touch any ball from within the playing area that is on its downward flight with an opportunity to score.” and “During a field goal attempt, touch a ball, which has a chance to score, after it has touched any part of the backboard above ring level, whether the ball is considered on its upward or downward flight.” and “Touch any ball from within the playing area when it is above the basket ring and within the imaginary cylinder.”



Length of the game
How long a game is and how it is divided; the one rule every other clock hangs on. Entry.
Four periods of twelve minutes; overtime periods of five minutes. Rule No. 5, Section II

Verbatim: “All periods of regulation play in the NBA will be twelve minutes.” and “All overtime periods of play will be five minutes.”



Shot clock
The time a team has to attempt a shot that reaches the ring; the number that sets the pace of every possession. Entry.
24 seconds. Rule No. 7, Section I

Verbatim: “The shot clock shall start at 24 seconds unless otherwise provided in Rule 7.”



Three-point line
How far the arc is from the basket, and how far the corner line is from the sideline; the geometry every spacing decision in Chapter 3 rests on. Entry.
An arc of 23 feet 9 inches from the middle of the basket, meeting lines 3 feet from the sidelines. Rule No. 1, Section I

Verbatim, in the page’s own characters: “The three-point field goal area has parallel lines 3’ from the sidelines, extending from the baseline and an arc of 23’9” from the middle of the basket which intersects the parallel lines.”

title: Rules compared
text:
The same rule across five rule sets. Every cell is one of three things: a value with the rule or article number it comes from, linked to the document on file; a stated absence, where the document was read for that concept and has no such rule; or a stated gap, where the league’s text is not public and the page searched is named. Nothing here is inferred from another league or filled from memory. The per-league pages carry the same cells with the verbatim words each rests on.

title: Roles
text:
The five numbers, and the blended roles that replaced them.
All families · 7 terms · 0 full, 0 partial, 7 short

Center (5)
Also: the five, the big
The primary screener, roller and rim protector.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Rim runner, Drop coverage


Combo guard
A guard who moves between initiating and spacing without a fixed role.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Point guard (1)


Point forward
A forward-sized player who runs the offense, which puts a bigger defender at the point of attack.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Point guard (1), Mismatch


Point guard (1)
The primary ball-handler and initiator.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Combo guard, Point forward


Power forward (4)
Also: stretch four
The second big; today often a perimeter player who screens, pops and makes short-roll decisions.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Short roll, Pop


Shooting guard (2)
The secondary handler and primary perimeter scorer; today mostly an off-ball mover and spacer.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10


Small forward (3)
The wing; expected to shoot, drive and defend several positions.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10

title: Pick-and-roll coverages
text:
How two defenders handle a ball screen. This decides a team’s defensive identity.
All families · 9 terms · 9 full, 0 partial, 0 short

At the level
The big meets the handler at the level of the screen, between drop and hedge.

Why it is run. Meeting the handler at the screen takes away both the pull-up the drop concedes and the corner the hedge risks, and asks the big to be quick for one beat rather than far from the rim for several.
What beats it. The short roll, which gives the screener the pocket pass while the big is still turning; the slip, which goes before the big has arrived at the level.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage, Hedge


Blitz
Also: trap, double team
Both defenders trap the handler at the screen, leaving three defenders against four.

Why it is run. Two defenders on the handler take the ball out of the one player’s hands the defense fears most, and hand it to a screener at the free-throw line who, the defense is betting, cannot make the next decision.
What beats it. The short roll, built for exactly this; the pop to a screener who shoots; a handler who splits the trap.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Short roll, 4-on-3, Hedge


Drop coverage
Also: drop
Against a ball screen the big stays back near the paint while the guard fights over the screen.

Why it is run. Keeping the big back between the ball and the rim takes away the layup and the lob, which are the two best shots a ball screen produces, and asks the big to do only what he does best: guard the rim without moving his feet in space.
What beats it. A handler who makes the mid-range pull-up or the pull-up three the drop leaves; the snake, which walks the drop into the paint; the lob when the big commits early.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Pick-and-roll, Snake dribble, Ice


Hedge
Also: show, hard hedge
The big jumps out above the screen to stop the handler, then recovers to the roller.

Why it is run. Jumping the big out above the screen stops the handler from turning the corner at all, which against a scorer who must not get downhill is worth the roller it leaves open for a beat.
What beats it. The slip before the show; the short roll into a 4-on-3 while the big is out; the pop when he commits; the Spain back screen on his way home.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage, Blitz


Ice
Also: blue, down, push, iced
On a side ball screen the on-ball defender forces the handler toward the sideline and away from the screen, with the big dropped toward the baseline.

Why it is run. Refusing the screen and sending the handler down the sideline turns a two-man action into a one-man drive into a wall, with the whole weak side behind the ball and hard to reach.
What beats it. The step-up screen, set so the way the guard is forcing is the way the screen goes; the pop by the unused screener; a shooter in the ice-side corner, who turns the drive into a kick-out.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage, Step-up screen


Man-to-man
Each defender is responsible for one attacker wherever he goes.

Why it is run. One defender per attacker is the arrangement that guards every shooter and every driver at once, and the ball screen is the one action that makes two of those assignments collide; every coverage is a rule for that collision.
What beats it. Any action that keeps two attackers on one defender longer than the coverage’s rule covers: a late-guarded pick-and-roll, or the mismatch hunted after a switch.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Zone defense, Switch


Next
Also: next switch, up-to-touch
A switch called by the big on a ball screen where the guard’s defender stays attached until the big has the handler.

Why it is run. A switch has one weak moment, the trade, and keeping the guard attached until the big has touched the handler removes it; there is no step in which the ball is guarded by nobody.
What beats it. The slip, which gives the big nothing to be level with; the ghost screen, which draws the call and vanishes.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.5 · See also Switch


Switch
The two defenders in a screen trade assignments.

Why it is run. Trading men at the screen means nobody is ever beaten, so nothing has to rotate; the screen produces a mismatch and nothing else, and the defense is betting the mismatch is the smaller problem.
What beats it. The mismatch hunted before it is fixed: the early seal by the big, the isolation of the guard against the big, and the slip before the switch is called.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.5 · See also Scram switch, Mismatch, Peel switch


Under
Also: go under
The on-ball defender goes beneath the screen, conceding the pull-up to keep the drive in front.

Why it is run. Going beneath the screen keeps the drive in front of the guard without any help, at the price of the pull-up, and against a handler who will not make that shot the price is nothing.
What beats it. The shot, from any handler who has one; and the re-screen, since a defender under the screen can be screened again on his way back.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage

title: Off-ball screens
text:
Screens for players without the ball, which is how shooters get open.
All families · 11 terms · 11 full, 0 partial, 0 short

Back screen
A screen set behind a defender, out of his view, so the cutter can go to the rim.

Why it is run. A defender watching the ball cannot see a screen set on his back, so the man he guards is at the rim before he can follow.
What beats it. Feeling the screen and going under it toward the rim early, conceding the pop, or switching every back screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Flare screen, Rip screen, Spain pick-and-roll


Cross screen
A screen set across the lane so a big can cut from one block to the other for a post catch.

Why it is run. A screen across the lane, block to block, gets a big a post catch with his defender sealed on his back, because the defender must choose between going over the screen and going under it into the passing lane.
What beats it. The defender going over the top to reach the block first and fronting the post, or a low man who bumps the cutter in the lane.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Post-up, Block


Elevator screen
Also: elevator doors
A shooter runs between two screeners who then step together to close the gap on his defender.

Why it is run. Two screeners who close the gap the moment the shooter is through stop his defender dead with two bodies at once, and it is the one screen set after the cutter has passed.
What beats it. Going round the outside of one screener before the doors close, conceding a step on the catch, or switching one screener’s defender onto the shooter as he comes through.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Stagger


Flare screen
A screen that lets a perimeter player fade away from the ball along the arc, punishing a defender who cheats toward the ball.

Why it is run. A defender who cheats toward the ball can be screened on the side facing away from it, so his man fades along the arc for a skip pass the defense was leaning away from.
What beats it. A defender who stays on the line between his man and the ball and never cheats, or a switch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Pin-down, Back screen


Floppy
A shooter under the rim chooses either side, one with a single screen and one with a stagger.

Why it is run. A shooter under the rim with a single screen one way and a stagger the other reads his defender’s first step and goes the other way; the defender cannot be right about both sides.
What beats it. Going under everything and meeting him at the wing, conceding the curl, or switching every screen so a fresh defender waits on either side.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Stagger, Pin-down


Hammer
A baseline drive on one side with a back screen on the other, freeing a shooter into the weak-side corner for a drift pass.

Why it is run. The weak-side helper who sinks on a baseline drive is doing what he was taught, and the back screen punishes him for it; the shooter drifts to the corner and the pass comes along the baseline under the rim.
What beats it. Helping with the eyes and not the feet, so the shooter is never left, or the X-out rotation in which the big’s defender takes the corner and the wing defender takes the big.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Back screen, Corner


Loop
A cutter running a triple stagger along the baseline from one wing to the other.

Why it is run. Three screens along a path the defender must run in full, with the catch waiting at the far wing.
What beats it. Cutting across the lane under the screens to meet the cutter at the far wing, conceding the curl on the first screen, or a switch at any of the three.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Stagger


Pin-down
Also: down screen
A screen set facing the baseline so a player near the rim can cut up to the perimeter for a catch.

Why it is run. A screen facing the baseline lets a shooter who started near the rim arrive at the perimeter with his defender behind the screen, and gives him four reads off it (curl, fade, straight, back cut) that the defender’s choice decides.
What beats it. Top-locking the shooter so he cannot reach the screen, conceding the back cut to take away the shot, or switching the screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Flare screen, Stagger, Top-lock


Rip screen
A back screen across the lane, usually for a player who has just set a screen himself.

Why it is run. A defender who has just helped on a screen is standing exactly where a back screen wants him, so the screener he left rips to the rim behind him.
What beats it. The screener’s defender never leaving him to help, or a switch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Back screen


Stagger
Also: staggered screens
Two off-ball screens in a row in the same direction for one cutter.

Why it is run. Two screens in the same direction make the defender right twice; the wrong side of the first is the wrong side of the second, and the second screener can slip if his own defender jumps out.
What beats it. Going under both screens and meeting the shooter at the catch, conceding the curl, or switching the second screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Pin-down, Floppy


Wedge
A player receives an off-ball screen to the top and immediately turns to set a ball screen.

Why it is run. A side screen for the big before he screens the ball makes his defender late to the pick-and-roll, the same idea as the ram from a different direction.
What beats it. Switching the first screen so the nearest defender guards the ball screen, or the big’s defender going under the first screen and beating him to the top.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Pick-and-roll, Ram

title: Reference
text: Every term on the site, grouped by family and then listed A to Z. Each entry says what the thing is in one sentence and names the lecture that teaches it, which is where the diagram and the counter live. Use the search box for a word you heard and do not know. The count after each family is full / partial / short: full means the entry says why it is run and what beats it.

title: Reference
text:
By family

The floor and spacing (0 / 1 / 15 of 16). Where things are, and why five players standing in the right places is most of offense.
Roles (0 / 0 / 7 of 7). The five numbers, and the blended roles that replaced them.
Transition offense (14 / 0 / 0 of 14). Scoring before the defense is set.
Transition defense (11 / 2 / 0 of 13). Rim, ball, then match up. In that order.
Early offense (2 / 0 / 0 of 2). The first action after the break, against a defense that is back but not organized.
On-ball screens (12 / 0 / 2 of 14). Screens for the player with the ball, and the family that grew out of the pick-and-roll.
Off-ball screens (11 / 0 / 0 of 11). Screens for players without the ball, which is how shooters get open.
Cuts and actions (16 / 0 / 3 of 19). The movements that are not screens: handoffs, cuts, seals, drives and the passes that follow.
Sets and systems (12 / 1 / 1 of 14). Alignments, called plays, and the rule-based offenses that run without a call.
Pick-and-roll coverages (9 / 0 / 0 of 9). How two defenders handle a ball screen. This decides a team’s defensive identity.
Help and rotations (13 / 0 / 0 of 13). What the other three defenders do when the first two are beaten.
Zones and junk defenses (9 / 0 / 1 of 10). Guarding areas instead of players, and hybrids built to erase one scorer.
Presses (1 / 0 / 0 of 1). Full-court and three-quarter-court pressure, and what it is built to force.
Special situations (6 / 0 / 2 of 8). Inbounds, timeouts, presses and zone offense.
Late clock and endgame (3 / 1 / 0 of 4). What changes when the clock, not the defense, is the constraint.
Analytics and trends (1 / 1 / 1 of 3). The measurements behind the choices, and what has changed recently. Every claim here carries a source.
Rules and regulations (0 / 0 / 9 of 9). Rules with no tactical home of their own: the clock, the counts, the timeouts. Every cell cites a rulebook.

title: Early offense
text:
The first action after the break, against a defense that is back but not organized.
All families · 2 terms · 2 full, 0 partial, 0 short

Early offense
Actions run in the first seconds of a half-court possession, against a defense that is back but not yet organized.
Why it is run. A defense that got back has still not matched up, and its big is often trailing. Early offense hits that seam with one quick action before the defense settles.
What beats it. Matching up while sprinting back, and having the big sprint rather than jog.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Drag screen, Pistol, Delay, Secondary break


Trailer flip
The trailing big arriving at the top to take a reversal pass and swing the ball to the other side.
Why it is run. The trailing big is the one attacker the defense has not matched; taking the reversal at the top and swinging it in one motion gets the ball to the weak side before the defense has shifted.
What beats it. The big’s defender sprinting to the top with him so the reversal is contested, or the weak-side defenders shifting on the flight of the first pass.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Trailer, Delay

title: The floor and spacing
text:
Where things are, and why five players standing in the right places is most of offense.
All families · 16 terms · 0 full, 1 partial, 15 short

4-out 1-in
An alignment with four players outside the arc and one inside, usually in the dunker spot or on a block.

offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also 5-out, Dunker spot


5-out
An alignment with all five players outside the arc and the paint empty.

offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also 4-out 1-in, Spacing, Delay


Block
The painted mark on the lane line near the rim; the traditional low-post spot.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Post-up, Dunker spot


Corner
Also: weak corner
The spot where the three-point line meets the sideline; the closest three to the rim, and the spot the low man has to leave to help. The weak corner is the one on the help side, which is why it is the open one.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Low man, Corner three, Weak side


Dunker spot
Also: short corner
The baseline spot just outside the lane, below the block, where a non-shooting big waits for lobs, dump-offs and offensive rebounds.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Block, Lob


Elbow
Where the free-throw line meets the lane line; a hub for handoffs and high-post play.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Pinch post, Horns


Gap
Also: double gap, single gap
The space between two perimeter players; a single gap is one spot wide, a double gap is two, and a driver wants the double.

offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Spacing, Drive


Nail
The middle of the free-throw line; the help spot that threatens a drive from either side.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Help side, Dig, Stunt


Restricted area
The half-circle in front of the rim inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also The paint, Verticality


Slot
The perimeter spot above the arc roughly in line with the lane line, between the top and the wing.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Wing, Top of the key, Corner


Spacing
Keeping players far enough apart that one defender cannot guard two of them.
Why it is run. Standing so that no defender can guard two attackers at once is what makes every drive, cut and screen in this chapter work; the measurement is the gap, and a double gap is the one worth attacking.
offense · General · partial · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also 5-out, Gap


Strong side
Also: ball side
The half of the floor, split lengthwise, that the ball is on.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Weak side, Help side


The paint
Also: the key, the lane
The rectangle from the baseline to the free-throw line, bounded by the lane lines; the highest-value shots come from here.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Restricted area, Block, Dunker spot


Top of the key
Also: top
The perimeter spot straight out from the rim, above the arc.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Slot


Weak side
Also: help side
The half of the floor, split lengthwise, away from the ball; on defense this is where help comes from.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Strong side, Low man, Tag


Wing
The perimeter spot roughly level with the free-throw line extended.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Slot, Corner

title: Read a possession
text:
The front page opens with a sentence somebody says in a room:
That is about ten seconds of basketball, and it is six pieces of vocabulary, two decisions and one consequence. This page takes it apart in the order it happened. Every phrase links to its entry, which has the definition and the picture, and to the lecture that teaches it.
If you read nothing else on this site, read this page. It is the whole thing in miniature: an action, the coverage chosen to stop it, the help that coverage requires, and the shot the offense gets because that help had to come from somewhere.

title: Read a possession
text:
“the drag”
Start with what the offense did. A drag screen is a ball screen set in transition by a trailing big, before the defense is set. It is the first action of lecture 3.2, and its whole value is timing: the screener arrives at the arc a step before his own defender does, so for one beat the two defenders in the screen have no agreed answer to it.
Nothing has gone wrong for the defense yet. A drag is a question, asked early.

title: Read a possession
text:
“they iced”
Here is the first decision, and it belongs to two defenders. Ice is a pick-and-roll coverage: the on-ball defender jumps to the high side of the handler, between him and the screen, and forces the dribble down the sideline instead of into the middle. The big drops below the screen to meet the drive. The screen is refused rather than fought over. It is one of six coverages in lecture 4.3, and choosing it says something specific: this defense would rather give up a baseline drive than a handler coming downhill through the middle of the floor.
Against a drag, icing is also a race, because the big has to get level with the screen before it is set. That is the subject of lecture 4.2.
So far the possession is two defenders doing their jobs. The sentence has not yet said anything went wrong.

title: Read a possession
text:
“and the low man tagged”
Now the third defender. The low man is the weak-side defender nearest the baseline, and in every coverage on this site he is the one with two jobs: guard his own man in the corner, and meet whatever comes to the rim. When the screener rolls, there is a beat when the roller is between the two defenders in the screen and neither can reach him. The tag is the low man stepping into the lane to bump the roller for that beat and then leaving again.
It is a delay, not a switch, and it is taught in lecture 4.4. It is also the moment the possession turns, because the low man cannot be in two places, and the sentence is about to say where he was not.

title: Read a possession
text:
“so 5 short-rolled”
The offense’s answer. A short roll is the screener cutting off his roll, stopping around the free-throw line instead of running to the rim, and catching the ball there. He does it precisely because the defense committed two players to the ball and a third to tagging him: catching short puts him behind the first two and in front of the third, with the ball, facing a defense that is now three against four. That arithmetic is 4-on-3, and both are in lecture 3.3.
The word so in the sentence is doing real work. The short roll is not a separate idea from the tag; it is the counter to it.

title: Read a possession
text:
“and hit the weak corner”
And the shot. The weak corner is the corner on the help side, and it is the shot the modern offense is built to find for one reason: it is the spot the low man had to leave in order to tag. The corner is the shortest three on the floor, taught with the rest of the floor in lecture 3.10, and the pass to it out of a short roll is the kick-out of the same lecture.
Nobody was beaten. Every defender did the job his coverage gave him. The offense took a rule the defense had agreed on in advance and made it produce an open shot, which is what a good offense does and why the defense has to choose between coverages rather than find a correct one.

title: Read a possession
section: What to notice, if you watch the next one live
text:
What to notice, if you watch the next one live
Three things, in this order, and none of them is the ball.
Where the big goes when the screen is set. Backward is drop or ice; still at the screen is at the level; forward is a hedge or a blitz. That one step tells you the defense’s whole plan for the possession, and it happens before anybody shoots.
Which defender leaves first. Help has to come from somewhere, and the somewhere is a man. Watch who steps in, and you know which shot is about to be open, a beat before the pass.
What the offense does second. The first action rarely scores. The short roll, the kick-out and the skip pass are all second actions, and a possession is usually decided by whether the offense has one.

title: Read a possession
text:
Where to go next
The four chapters, in the order a possession happens:

Chapter 1, where the game came from, five eras bounded by dated rule changes.
Chapter 2, how it is played now, measured, with every number sourced or marked as a gap.
Chapter 3, the offense, from the break to the late clock.
Chapter 4, the defense that answers it, in the same order.

Or start from a word you heard: the Reference lists every term A to Z, each with its definition, its picture, and the lecture that teaches it.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
New terms introduced (10): 1-2-2 zone, 1-3-1 zone, 2-3 zone, 3-2 zone, Box-and-one, Diamond-and-one, Junk defense, Match-up zone, Triangle-and-two, Zone defense. Diagrams: 10.
Everything in lectures 4.3 to 4.5 assumed that each defender had a man. A zone drops the assumption. Each defender is responsible for an area of the floor and for whoever is in it, and when an attacker leaves the area he stops being that defender’s problem. The screen, which was the whole subject of 4.3, does almost nothing to a zone, because there is no assignment to collide. What the zone gives up in exchange is the arithmetic of the perimeter: five areas cannot cover the whole arc, and an offense that moves the ball faster than the zone moves its bodies gets an open three somewhere on every possession.
Section 1 is the zone as a decision and what every zone concedes. Sections 2 to 5 are the four shapes a viewer will see, the 2-3, the 3-2, the 1-2-2 and the 1-3-1, each with the picture of where it is thick and where it is thin. Section 6 is the match-up zone, which tries to have both. Section 7 is the junk defenses, the box-and-one and the triangle-and-two, which are zones with a grudge.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
1 Guarding areas
A zone is chosen for one of three reasons. The first is protection: a defense that cannot stay in front of the other team’s drivers packs the paint and makes them shoot over it. The second is personnel: a team with a slow big who cannot guard a ball screen puts him in the middle of a zone where the ball screen does not exist. The third is disruption: an offense that has practiced against man-to-man all week sees a zone and has to think, and thinking is slow. Zones are far more common below the professional level for all three reasons, and rare at the top because professional shooters make the zone’s one concession too expensive.
That concession is the same in every shape. A zone guards the paint with more bodies than man-to-man can and the arc with fewer, so it gives up the outside shot and the skip pass, and it gives up offensive rebounds, because no defender has a man to box out. Zone offense, the subject of lecture 3.12, is the list of ways to collect on those: the ball in the high post where two areas meet, the short corner behind the baseline defenders, the overload that puts three attackers in two areas, and the skip pass across the whole zone to the side it has just left.






Assignment


Each defender guards an area and whoever enters it. The ball is guarded by whichever area it is in; the others shift toward it, so the zone is always tilted to the ball side.


Concedes


The outside shot, the skip pass to the far side, and the offensive rebound. Every shape below trades a different piece of the arc for a different piece of the paint.


Requires


Five players who shift together on every pass and talk through every cutter. A zone that moves late is five men standing in five spots.


Beaten by


Zone offense: the high-post entry, the short corner, the overload, and the skip pass to the side the zone has just left.





Coverage 1: Zone: guard the floor, not the man, and pay for it at the arc and on the glass.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
2 The 2-3
The 2-3 zone is the most common zone in the game and the one the word usually means (Figure 1). Two defenders stand above the free-throw line, one either side of the lane, and three stand across the lane near the blocks and in front of the rim. It packs the paint completely: a drive from anywhere meets a defender at the end of it, and the rim is guarded by a big who never leaves.






Figure 1: The 2-3 zone. Two guards up, three across the back. Every drive ends at a defender. The high post, where the two lines meet, and the corners, which the back line has to stretch to reach, are where it is thin.



It is thin in two places. The high post, at the free-throw line, sits exactly between the front two and the back three, and a player who catches there has a defender coming from each direction and neither arriving first. The corners are the back line’s responsibility, and the back-line defender who runs to a corner shooter has left the block behind him empty. The 2-3’s whole vulnerability is the pass from the high post to the corner, and lecture 3.12’s zone offense is built to throw it.






Assignment


Two up, three back. The front pair guards the top and the wings; the back three guard the blocks and the rim and slide to the corners.


Concedes


The high post and the corner three, and the offensive glass.


Requires


A back line that talks, since three players share the corners and the rim, and a middle defender who never leaves the paint.


Beaten by


Zone offense through the high post: the catch at the free-throw line, then the pass to the corner the back line has to stretch to, and the skip pass when the whole zone has shifted.





Coverage 2: The 2-3: the paint is closed and the high post is the key to it.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
3 The 3-2
The 3-2 zone turns the 2-3 upside down (Figure 2). Three defenders stand across the free-throw line extended, one at the top and one on each side, and two stand near the blocks. The arc is crowded and hard to shoot over, which is why a defense chooses it against a team of perimeter shooters. Behind the three, the two low defenders have the whole baseline and the glass to themselves.






Figure 2: The 3-2 zone. Three across the free-throw line extended, two on the blocks. The arc is crowded; the baseline and the glass belong to two players.



It is thin where the 2-3 is thick. The high post is guarded, because the top defender is standing near it, but the short corners and the baseline are two players’ responsibility and the offensive rebound is theirs to lose. A team that shoots badly and rebounds well is the 3-2’s worst opponent.






Assignment


Three across the top, two on the blocks. The top three take away the arc and the high post; the low two guard the baseline and the rim.


Concedes


The short corner, the baseline drive, and the offensive rebound against a bigger team.


Requires


Two low defenders who can guard the whole baseline and rebound against five.


Beaten by


Zone offense along the baseline: the short-corner catch behind the low pair, and the drive into the gap between a top defender and a low one.





Coverage 3: The 3-2: the arc is closed and the baseline is the price.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
4 The 1-2-2
The 1-2-2 zone is the shape between them (Figure 3). One defender at the top, two at the elbows, two on the blocks. From the top it looks like a 3-2 and from the baseline like a 2-3, and it shifts into either: when the ball goes to a wing, the elbow defender on that side steps out and the shape is a 2-3 tilted to the ball; when the ball is at the top, the point defender and the two elbows are a three-man front. It covers the arc better than the 2-3 and the baseline better than the 3-2, and it does neither as well as the shape built for it.






Figure 3: The 1-2-2 zone. One at the top, two at the elbows, two on the blocks. It becomes a 2-3 on a wing entry and a three-man front when the ball is at the top, and is thinnest in the short corner and at the elbows’ outside shoulder.









Assignment


One up, two at the elbows, two on the blocks. The elbow defender on the ball side steps out to the wing; the point defender guards the top and drops to the high post when the ball goes to a wing.


Concedes


The short corner and the wing three when the elbow defender is late stepping out.


Requires


Two elbow defenders who can guard a wing and recover to the high post, which is a lot of ground.


Beaten by


The quick wing-to-corner pass before the elbow defender has stepped out, and the same high-post and short-corner attacks that beat the 2-3.





Coverage 4: The 1-2-2: a 2-3 from the baseline, a 3-2 from the top, and thinner than either at its own edges.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
5 The 1-3-1
The 1-3-1 zone is a different kind of zone, because it is not built to protect (Figure 4). One defender stands at the point above the arc, three stand across the free-throw line with the middle one at the line itself, and one, the baseline runner, covers the whole baseline alone. Its purpose is to trap. When the ball goes to a wing, the point defender and the wing defender converge on it; when it goes to a corner, the wing defender and the baseline runner do. The shape is long and thin, it invites the pass to the wing, and it punishes the handler who catches there and holds the ball.






Figure 4: The 1-3-1 zone. A point, three across the free-throw line, and one runner along the baseline. The ball has gone to the wing and the point and wing defenders trap it; the runner slides to take the corner. The shape exists to force the long pass.



The 1-3-1 concedes the corners, because a single baseline runner cannot be in both, and it concedes the skip pass, because the trap has committed two defenders to one side. It is a gambling zone: it produces turnovers against a team that panics in the trap, and open corner threes against one that does not.






Assignment


Point, three across, one runner. The point and the ball-side wing trap the wing catch; the runner covers whichever corner the ball is nearer; the middle defender guards the high post and the rim.


Concedes


The far corner, the skip pass out of the trap, and the offensive rebound; only one defender starts near the baseline.


Requires


A baseline runner who can cover corner to corner, and trappers who arrive together and do not foul.


Beaten by


The skip pass out of the trap to the far corner, and a handler who keeps his dribble alive and splits the trap.





Coverage 5: The 1-3-1: a trap with a shape, and a corner three at the end of every pass out of it.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
6 The match-up zone
The match-up zone tries to keep what a zone is good at and remove what it is bad at (Figure 5). It starts in a zone shape, usually a 2-3 or a 1-2-2. But inside the shape, each defender guards the attacker in his area man to man for as long as the attacker is there, denying the pass and following the cut, and when the attacker leaves the area he is handed to the next defender the way a zone hands off. The offense sees a man-to-man defender on every catch and a zone on every pass, and an offense that runs its zone offense finds bodies on its shooters while one that runs its man offense finds its screens doing nothing.






Figure 5: Match-up zone. A 2-3 shape. A cutter comes through the lane from the left wing toward the right corner; the left-back defender takes him man to man through his area and hands him to the right-back defender at the edge of it. Man on every cutter, zone on every pass.



It is the hardest defense in this lecture to play, because every hand-off is a conversation, and the defense that does not talk gives up a cutter every time. Its concession is the seams: the moment of the hand-off, when a cutter is between two areas and the two defenders have not yet agreed whose he is.






Assignment


Zone shape, man principles inside it. Guard the attacker in your area as a man; hand him to the next area when he leaves; take whoever arrives.


Concedes


The cutter at the seam, during the hand-off; and whatever the base shape concedes.


Requires


Constant talk, and five defenders who can each guard any attacker one-on-one for a few seconds.


Beaten by


Cutters through the seams faster than the hand-off can be made, and an overload that puts two attackers in one area at once.





Coverage 6: Match-up zone: man on the catch, zone on the pass, and every seam is a conversation.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
text:
7 Junk defenses
A junk defense is a zone-and-man hybrid built to take one or two players out of a game. It is also called a combination defense. It concedes that the other team has a scorer the defense cannot guard within a normal scheme, assigns one defender to that scorer full time, and guards the other four attackers with a zone of the remaining four defenders. The bet is that the other four attackers cannot beat a four-man zone, and it is a bet made against teams with one star and little around him, which is why junk defenses are common in high school and college and almost unheard of in a league where every roster has three players who can score.
The box-and-one is the common form (Figure 6). Four defenders form a box, two at the elbows and two near the blocks, and the fifth stands face to face with the scorer and follows him everywhere, ignoring the ball entirely. The scorer never catches without a defender in his chest, and if he does catch he is met by the box as well.






Figure 6: Box-and-one. Four defenders in a box, two at the elbows and two on the blocks; the fifth follows the opponent’s scorer face to face and ignores the ball. Everyone else is guarded by an area.



The diamond-and-one is the box with its four zone defenders turned forty-five degrees (Figure 7): one at the free-throw line, one on each side of the lane, one in front of the rim. It guards the top of the key and the rim better than the box and the blocks and the short corners worse, and a defense chooses between them by where the other four attackers like to shoot from.






Figure 7: Diamond-and-one. The same chaser on the same scorer; behind him the four zone defenders form a diamond rather than a box, one at the free-throw line, one on each side of the lane, one in front of the rim.



The triangle-and-two is the same idea against two scorers (Figure 8). Two defenders chase, and the remaining three form a triangle, one at the free-throw line and two near the blocks. Three defenders cannot guard the arc, so it concedes the outside shot to the other three attackers entirely, and it is played only when the defense is sure those three cannot make it.






Figure 8: Triangle-and-two. Two chasers face to face with the two scorers, and a triangle behind them: one at the free-throw line, two near the blocks. The three other attackers are guarded by areas only, and the arc belongs to them.



Every junk defense concedes the same thing in the end: the players it is not guarding. The box gives up the shots of the four attackers who are not the star, the triangle gives up the arc to the three who are not the two scorers, and both are beaten the moment a player the defense chose to ignore proves he should not have been. The scorer’s own counter is to screen: a chased player who sets a screen drags his chaser into a collision with the box, and the box has no rule for that.






Assignment


One or two defenders chase the scorers face to face and ignore the ball; the rest form a box or a triangle zone and guard everyone else by area.


Concedes


The shots of the attackers the defense chose not to chase, and the offensive glass.


Requires


A chaser with the stamina to deny one man for forty minutes, and an opponent whose other players cannot punish the zone behind him.


Beaten by


The unchased players scoring; the chased scorer setting screens, which the zone has no rule for; and the post-up of a big against a four-man zone that has no one to double.





Coverage 7: Junk defenses: erase one player, and hope the other four are the players you think they are.

title: 4.6: Zones and Junk Defenses
section: 8 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
text:
8 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
The glossaries this site draws on name one more junk defense, described by one publisher only, so under this site’s rule it has no entry until a second independent source names it. The description is given here so the word is not a mystery when it is heard; the rule and the dated diff behind it are in the plan (plan/PLAN.md, section 8.4) and data/sources/glossary_diff_2026-09-21.md. The diamond-and-one above was in this list until a second glossary named it on 2026-09-21; that is how a name moves from here to an entry.

Amoeba defense. A junk defense shaped like a 1-3-1, built to confuse and force turnovers rather than to protect; the one glossary that describes it calls it “A junk defense made popular by coach Jerry Tarkanian at UNLV.”1 Named by one publisher.

The idea to carry into lecture 4.7 is that the 1-3-1 was a zone built to trap, and a trap needs the ball to come to it. The next lecture is about defenses that go and get the ball instead, in the back court, before the offense has arrived at all.
