title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
section: 5 Movements that keep the floor spaced
text:
5 Movements that keep the floor spaced
Two entries in this lecture are not cuts to score. They are movements a player makes so that the cuts and drives around him work.
The lift is the corner player’s move when the ball is driven baseline on his side. If he stays in the corner, the driver has no pass: the defender who helps on the drive comes from the corner, and the corner is then covered by the rim protector’s rotation. If he lifts to the wing as the drive starts, he is a kick-out target the help defender has to leave to guard, and the drive gets a second option. The lift is a spacing rule, not a cut: the player is moving to stay one pass away from the ball.
The pinch post is the big catching at the weak-side elbow, facing the ball, with nobody else on his side of the floor. From there he has a handoff for a guard cutting past him, a shot, a drive, or the pass to a back cutter, and the offenses that use it, the Princeton and the triangle of lecture 3.9, use it as the hub of everything on that side. It is a spot as much as an action, and it is named here so that the phrase means something when it is heard.
crumbs: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
section: 6 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
text:
6 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
The glossaries describe several more cuts and post actions by one publisher only, so each has a description here and no entry until a second source names it. The diff is data/sources/glossary_diff_2026-09-21.md.

Curl, fade, straight, and the V-cut and L-cut. The first three are the reads off a screen taught in lecture 3.5. A V-cut is a perimeter player stepping in toward the rim and exploding back out to receive; an L-cut runs up the lane line and out to the wing. They are how a player without a screen gets open for a perimeter catch.
Shallow cut. A cut made in front of the ball to a new spot beside the handler, so the two exchange positions; the wave is its cousin, a cut made to create a double gap.
Rub and brush screen. A cut made so the cutter or his defender gets in the path of a different defender without contact, so it works like a screen but is not one under the rules.
Duck-in. A post player stepping into the lane and sealing his defender with his inside foot the moment the defender is in a help position.
Slice. A cut from the opposite corner through the lane, sometimes off a screen, to the top of the key.
Split cut. After a post entry, the two perimeter players nearest the post screen for one another and cut in opposite directions, so the post has two cutters to read.
Barkley. Dribbling from the perimeter into the block for a post-up, as the player it is named for did.
Boomerang. A pass to a teammate followed by an immediate return pass, so the original handler has a live dribble again, usually to attack a mismatch after a switch.
Dive, reverse seal, basket cut. A dive is a cut from the high post to the low post; a reverse seal is the low post holding his defender on the outside hip as the ball is reversed, which is the seal the high-low depends on; a basket cut is any hard cut to the rim.

The idea to carry into lecture 3.8 is that the screens of lectures 3.5 and 3.6 and the cuts of this one are what a team’s set plays are made of. The next lecture is about the sets themselves: the alignments a team starts from and the scripts it runs from them.
crumbs: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
New terms introduced (2): Corner three, Gravity. No diagrams.
Lecture 2.1 measured what changed. This lecture is about the measurement that caused it, and it is short, because the idea at its center is one division.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
1 Points per possession
Points per possession is points scored divided by possessions used. It is the currency of every argument in this site: a possession is the unit a team gets a fixed number of, so the only question about any action is how many points it returns per possession spent.
The reason this is the right unit and points per game is not is in the pace table of lecture 2.1. A team that plays fast scores more points per game without being better at scoring, and a team that plays slowly scores fewer without being worse. Dividing by possessions removes tempo from the comparison, which is what makes a 1979-80 offense and a 2024-25 offense comparable at all.
The figure this site already quotes for transition, in lecture 3.1, is of exactly this kind: a data set of college play-by-play since the 2010 season gives “the average points per transition play is 1.04” against “the average points per half-court play is 0.87”.1 That is a difference of 0.17 points per play, and everything in lecture 3.1 is a way of getting more plays into the first category.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
2 The arithmetic of the three
The whole of the shift measured in lecture 2.1 follows from one comparison, and it needs no data beyond the values of the shots.
A two-point shot made at rate p returns 2p points. A three-point shot made at rate q returns 3q. The three is the better shot whenever 3q > 2p, which is whenever q > (2/3)p. So a three taken at 35% returns 1.05 points, and a two must be made at better than 52.5% to match it.
That is the entire argument, and it was available on the day the line was adopted in 1979. What was missing for twenty years was not the arithmetic but the habit of counting. Lecture 2.1 shows the consequence: threes went from 3.1% of shots in 1979-80 to 42.2% in 2024-25, and true shooting rose from .531 to .576 over the same span.2

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
3 The corner three
The corner three is where that arithmetic is sharpest, and the reason is geometry rather than skill. The three-point line is a fixed arc around the basket with the corner segments cut off by the sidelines. The NBA rulebook states it in one sentence: “The three-point field goal area has parallel lines 3’ from the sidelines, extending from the baseline and an arc of 23’9” from the middle of the basket which intersects the parallel lines.”3 A shot from the corner is therefore taken from 22 feet rather than 23 feet 9 inches, the shortest three available, and worth the same three points.
That single fact is why the corner is a place in this site’s vocabulary rather than merely a region of the floor. The lift of lecture 3.7 exists to get a shooter out of it and back to the wing when the drive goes baseline; the kick-out and skip pass of lecture 3.10 exist to find him in it; the hammer of lecture 3.6 exists to put a shooter there against the grain of a defense’s rotation.

The corner three’s higher conversion rate is not sourced here. It is routinely reported that corner threes are made at a higher rate than threes from above the break, which is what the shorter distance would predict. This site has no shot-location table on file, for the reasons stated in lecture 2.1, so the claim appears here as the geometry (which is in the rulebook) and not as a conversion rate (which is not on file). What would close it: a public shot-location table by zone.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
4 Gravity
Gravity is the name for what a shooter does to defenders when he is not involved in the play. A defender who will not leave a shooter is a defender who is not helping, so the shooter’s presence is worth points scored by somebody else. It is the clearest case in this site of a term that exists because of a measurement: the idea that a player’s value can be located in shots he does not take requires someone to have counted what happens when he stands still.
Gravity is also why spacing is a property of a team rather than of a floor plan. Five players spread to the arc create nothing if their defenders can safely leave them; the same five spots occupied by shooters force every helper to make a choice. That is the difference between the 5-out alignment and 5-out as an offense.

Gravity is not quantified here. Several public and private analyses have put numbers on it. None of them is on file, so this lecture defines the term and does not measure it.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
section: 5 How much of the modern game is downstream of one division
text:
5 How much of the modern game is downstream of one division
A reader can draw a line from 3q > 2p through most of Chapter 3.

The floor. 5-out and 4-out 1-in exist to place shooters where help must come from.
The gap. Spacing is measured in gaps because a double gap is the distance a helper cannot cover in time, and it only matters if leaving the man costs three points rather than two.
The main action. The pick-and-roll of lecture 3.3 forces two defenders onto one attacker, and the pop exists because the screener’s defender now has to choose between the rim and the arc.
The shot chart. The corner three became a designed shot, and the drive and kick-out became the pair of actions that produce it.

What does not follow from it is anything in Chapter 1. The eras there are bounded by dated rule changes, and the arithmetic in this lecture was true in every one of them. That is the honest summary of this chapter: the sport did not learn a new fact in 2004, it started acting on an old one, and the measurements in lecture 2.1 are the record of it doing so.

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
This is the era the rest of this site is written about. Every action in Chapter 3 and every coverage in Chapter 4 is the current game, and the current game begins when the rules stopped guaranteeing an attacker one-on-one space and stopped allowing a defender to stand in the lane. What happened afterwards is that the sport spent twenty years discovering that the answer to both was spacing.
crumbs: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
section: 1 What the two rule changes did to the floor
text:
1 What the two rule changes did to the floor
Removing illegal defense allowed a defense to be anywhere. Defensive three seconds stopped it being in the lane, because a defender there must be “actively guarding an opponent within three seconds.”1 Together they replace one arrangement of the floor with another.
Under the old rules, an offense that cleared a side got a genuine one-on-one, because the defense was forbidden to zone up behind it. Under the new ones it does not, because help may come from anywhere; but help also cannot sit and wait at the rim. So the offense’s problem changes from “beat your man with no help coming” to “make the help come from somewhere it cannot afford to leave”. That is the whole of lecture 3.10: the gap, the drive, the kick-out, the skip pass.
Three consequences follow, and each is an entire lecture elsewhere on this site.
The pick-and-roll becomes the main action. A ball screen is the cheapest way to make two defenders guard one attacker, and the rules now permit the defense a dozen answers, which is why lecture 4.3 has six coverages in it and lecture 3.4 has five actions invented to beat them.
Spacing becomes the organizing idea. 5-out and 4-out 1-in exist to keep help far away, and the corner three becomes the shot an offense is built to produce because it is the shot the help defender has to leave to guard.
The big man’s job changes. The center of lecture 3.10 is a screener, a roller and a rim protector; the post-up that was the whole offense in lecture 1.3 becomes one option among many, used mostly against a mismatch.
crumbs: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
2 Nash and the Suns
The case for the current game was made publicly, and early, by one team.






Player


Steve Nash, point guard, Phoenix Suns


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 2, in 2004-05 and 2005-06.2 Hall of Fame, Class of 2018.3


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The player whose team made the case for pace and spacing in the first seasons after the paint opened, several years before the rest of the league agreed.





Player 1: Steve Nash: two MVP awards for playing the way the rules had just started to reward.



NBA.com’s review of the first of those seasons describes what it looked like at the time: “Nash set the league ablaze with a frenetic pace that resulted in a league-best 62 regular-season wins for the Phoenix Suns and an MVP award for Nash.”4 The word the page reaches for is pace, which is the measurement lecture 2.1 takes up.
crumbs: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
3 Duncan, and the era’s overlap
The other player carded here won the league’s highest individual award in the first two seasons after the rule change, playing the position the change was supposed to have devalued.






Player


Tim Duncan, forward, San Antonio Spurs


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 2, in 2001-02 and 2002-03.5 Finals Most Valuable Player, 3, in 1998-99, 2002-03 and 2004-05.6 Hall of Fame, Class of 2020.7


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The last player to win the league’s highest individual honor as a traditional big man on both sides of the rule change that opened the paint.





Player 2: Tim Duncan: MVP in the first two seasons of the new rules, and Finals MVP in the last season of the old ones.



His Finals MVP rows straddle the boundary: one in 1998-99, under the old rules, and two afterwards.8 That is worth stating because it is the honest version of what a rule change does. It does not end careers or reverse who is good. It changes what a team has to do to get a shot, and the players who were already good at the new thing get better.
crumbs: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
4 The take foul, 2022-23
One later rule change is on file with a primary source, and it is the one lecture 4.1 is built around. The league announced in July 2022 that “beginning with the 2022-23 NBA season” the penalty for a transition take foul would be that “the offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “the offensive team will retain possession of the ball.”9
It is a small rule with a clean mechanism: it made a tactic uneconomic rather than illegal. The team that fouls to stop a break now gives up a free throw and the ball, so the trade that made the foul worth it no longer works. That is the shape most modern rule changes take, and it is why this chapter’s boundaries are rule changes rather than trends: a rule changes the arithmetic on a specific day.

Hand-checking is not sourced here. The elimination of hand-checking is usually dated to 2004-05 and is usually named as a cause of the era’s scoring increase. NBA.com’s season review of 2004-05 is on file and does not mention it.10 So this lecture does not assert it. What would close the gap: the league’s own announcement of the rule change, or a rulebook edition carrying its adoption date.
crumbs: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
5 Where this chapter hands over
Chapter 1 has been about dates. Chapter 2 is about measurements: how much the three-point rate actually changed, what pace is now, where shots come from, and which of those claims this site can source and which it cannot. Chapters 3 and 4 are the game this era produced, action by action and coverage by coverage.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
The longest era in this chapter, and the one that most resembles the game as a set of principles rather than as a set of shots. Every possession now had a deadline; nothing yet rewarded shooting from distance. What the sport did with those twenty-five years is work out how to score near the rim against a defense that knew you had to.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
section: 1 What a possession without a three-point line is
text:
1 What a possession without a three-point line is
A modern viewer reading Chapter 3 might assume spacing is a permanent feature of basketball. It is not; it is a consequence of the three-point line, and this era is the proof. If every shot is worth two points, a shot from twenty-three feet is a worse version of a shot from ten, and there is no reason for an attacker to stand beyond the arc except to make room. Gap as a measurement means little when no defender is obliged to guard a man twenty-five feet from the rim.
So the offense of this era crowds the paint on purpose, the post-up is the central action, and the defense is built to stop shots close to the basket. The cross screen of lecture 3.5 and the high-low of lecture 3.7 are this era’s characteristic actions, and both exist to get one big man the ball on the block against another.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
2 Russell and Chamberlain
The era’s two defining players played the same position in opposite ways, and the league’s own year-by-year award lists record the result.






Player


Bill Russell, center, Boston Celtics


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 5, in 1957-58, 1960-61, 1961-62, 1962-63 and 1964-65.1 Hall of Fame, Class of 1975, as a player; the same list records a second induction as a coach, Class of 2021.2


Second bearing


The two inductions are confirmed as two by a second publisher.3


Why he mattered


The player who made defense the thing a team could be built on, in the era when the shot clock had just made every possession finite.





Player 1: Bill Russell: five MVP awards, and a second Hall of Fame induction forty-six years after the first.









Player


Wilt Chamberlain, center, Philadelphia Warriors, Philadelphia 76ers, Los Angeles Lakers


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 4, in 1959-60, 1965-66, 1966-67 and 1967-68.4 Finals Most Valuable Player, 1, in 1971-72.5 Hall of Fame, Class of 1979.6


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The other half of the era’s defining argument, and the player whose dominance produced more rule changes than any other.





Player 2: Wilt Chamberlain: four MVP awards, and one Finals MVP, because the award began in 1969.



The Finals MVP entry is worth pausing on, because it is a case where a count means less than it looks. NBA.com’s page states that “since 1969, the NBA has honored the NBA Finals’ best performer”,7 so a player whose best seasons were in the early 1960s could not have won it however he played. This is the clearest reason this chapter counts honors within an era rather than comparing totals across eras: the things being counted did not exist for the same length of time.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
section: 3 Abdul-Jabbar, and why a career is not an era
text:
3 Abdul-Jabbar, and why a career is not an era
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar’s six Most Valuable Player awards are the most on the league’s list, and they fall on both sides of this era’s ending: three with Milwaukee in the early 1970s and three with the Lakers, the last of them in 1979-80, the first season of the next era.8






Player


Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, center, Milwaukee Bucks, Los Angeles Lakers


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 6, in 1970-71, 1971-72, 1973-74, 1975-76, 1976-77 and 1979-80, which is more than any other name on the league’s list.9 Finals Most Valuable Player, 2, in 1970-71 and 1984-85.10 Hall of Fame, Class of 1995.11


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


A career that spans two of this chapter’s eras, which is the clearest evidence that an era boundary is a rule change rather than a change of personnel.





Player 3: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar: six MVP awards across two eras, and fourteen years between his two Finals MVPs.



That span is the argument for how this chapter is organized. If eras were defined by who was playing, Abdul-Jabbar’s career would be one era, and it would include both the game before the three-point line and the game after it. Because eras here are defined by dated rule changes, his career crosses a boundary, which is what a career is supposed to do.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
4 The ABA and the merger
The rival American Basketball Association operated through the back half of this era and ended in 1976, when several of its teams joined the NBA. Its lasting contribution is the line that ends this lecture: the three-point shot was an ABA feature before it was an NBA one.

The merger is not sourced here. This site has NBA.com’s season recaps for the boundary seasons on file, and none of them states the 1976 merger or its terms. The claim above about the ABA and the three-point line rests on the 1979-80 recap, which says the shot was “a popular facet of the ABA game”;12 the merger itself is stated here without a source on file, and will carry one or be removed when the sourcing pass for this chapter reaches it.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
5 The line
The era ends with a rule adopted from the competitor that had just folded into it. NBA.com’s review of 1979-80 records it plainly: “the 3-point field goal, a popular facet of the ABA game, was adopted by the league.”13 The same page notes what everyone remembers about that season instead: it “would forever be known as the year Larry Bird and Earvin” Magic Johnson arrived.14
Both things are true, and the ordering is the point of this chapter. The rookies are what the season is remembered for; the line is what changed the sport. The idea to carry into lecture 1.4 is that it did not change it at once: the next lecture is about the twenty years in which the line was on the floor and almost nobody shot from behind it.

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
Chapter 3 taught what a possession is made of and Chapter 4 will teach how it is stopped. This chapter is about where those things came from, and it is organized on one rule: an era begins and ends at a dated event, not at a change in how the basketball looked. A rule change is a date. A league merging with another is a date. “The game got faster in the sixties” is an impression, and impressions make boundaries that cannot be checked, so this chapter does not use them. Each era below is bounded by an event with a source, and where the date of an event is not on file, this site says so rather than guessing.
This lecture covers the first fifty-five years: one gymnasium, thirteen rules, and no professional league that lasted. Figure 1 is the whole chapter on one line, so the length of each era is visible before any of them is read. The first band is longer than the other four together, which is the fact about basketball history that a list of eras hides.

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
1 The invention
The game was invented on purpose, by one person, in response to a specific problem. Springfield College records that “the game was invented by Springfield College instructor and graduate student James Naismith in 1891”,1 and that the class it was invented for met in “the winter of 1891-1892”.2 Naismith had been given a class of restless students and a charge from Luther Gulick, the school’s physical education superintendent, to devise an indoor activity that would hold them.
What he produced was, in the college’s own account, an adaptation of several games then played: passing from American rugby, the jump ball from English rugby, the goal from lacrosse. He asked the janitor for two boxes and was given two peach baskets, which he nailed to the rail of the gymnasium’s running track. Then he “drew up the 13 original rules, which described, among other facets, the method of moving the ball and what constituted a foul.”3
Two things in that account matter for the rest of this site. The first is that the goal was horizontal and above the players’ heads, which is why nearly every action in Chapter 3 is about arriving at a spot rather than crossing a line. The second is that a foul was defined in the first thirteen rules, which is why the defensive vocabulary of Chapter 4 is so largely a vocabulary about what a defender may not do.

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
2 What the game looked like
For most of this era the game had two features that no modern viewer would recognize.
A center jump after every score. Possession was contested at the middle of the floor after each basket rather than handed to the conceding team, so a team with a dominant center could win possession repeatedly and a game could be a series of jump balls.
The set shot. The jump shot was not yet standard; the standard shot was taken with both feet on the floor. A game played with set shots from distance and a contested jump after every basket produced scores that look like misprints beside modern ones.
This is also the era in which the game spread furthest fastest, through the YMCA network and the colleges, and the reason it did is that the rules fitted on a page. Springfield College records that “a few weeks after the game was invented, students introduced the game at their own YMCAs.”4

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
3 The professional game before 1946
Professional leagues existed in this period and did not last. The one that ends this era is the Basketball Association of America, which played its first season in 1946-47 and is described by the league itself as “the precursor to the modern-day NBA”.5 That season was sixty games long, and NBA.com’s own account of it notes that “television was still in the future, and radio broadcasts were hardly universal.”6

No star cards in this era. The awards this chapter counts (Most Valuable Player, Finals Most Valuable Player) did not exist before the 1950s, and the only reachable primary source for a figure from this period is the Hall of Fame’s own inductee list, which gives a class year and no playing record. Rather than describe players from memory, this site leaves the era without star cards and names the gap. James Naismith is on that list as a contributor, in the Class of 1959, and he appears here as the inventor rather than as a player.

The idea to carry into lecture 1.2 is that the game had spread across a continent before anyone had built a professional league capable of surviving a decade. The next lecture is about the league that did, and about what it had to change to hold an audience.

title: Defense
text:
The defense’s job in one sentence: never let two defenders be needed on one player, and when they are, get the third defender there before the pass does. Every phase below is a different version of that race.


Defense lectures in reading order.


Lecture
What it teaches




4.1 Transition Defense
Rim, ball, match up; the tandem; floor balance and jamming the rebounder; the take foul before and after 2022-23.


4.2 Defending Early Offense
The coverages of 4.3 applied before the defense is set: getting level on the drag, switching the double drag, chasing the delay handoff, and matching up on the run.


4.3 Pick-and-Roll Coverages
Man-to-man as the frame; over and under; drop, ice, at the level, hedge and blitz, each as a card with what it concedes and what beats it.


4.4 Help and Rotations
The three defenders who are not in the screen: the help side and its two spots, the low man’s tag, the X-out, the stunt and the dig, the closeout, the top-lock, verticality, and the hit.


4.5 Switching Schemes
The switch as a coverage and as a scheme; next, the switch the big calls; the scram switch that fixes a post mismatch before the ball arrives; the peel switch that fixes a beaten defender.


4.6 Zones and Junk Defenses
Guarding areas instead of players: the 2-3, the 3-2, the 1-2-2 and the 1-3-1, what each shape is thin at; the match-up zone; and the junk defenses built to erase one or two scorers, the box-and-one and the triangle-and-two.


4.7 Presses
The press: pressure in the back court, what it is built to force, the trap on the sideline, the safety behind it, and why it is rare at the top of the game; the named presses the glossaries carry.


4.8 Special Situations, Defense
Defending the baseline and sideline inbounds: pressure the passer and the five-second count, switch everything, zone the inbound; and guarding the after-timeout play.


4.9 Late Clock, Defense
The foul as a tactic: the foul game that trades free throws for possessions, fouling up three, and hack-a, with what the rule book did to the last of these.



Terms by family: transition defense · pick-and-roll coverages · help and rotations · zones and junk.

title: Start here
text: This site is for the person in the room who hears “they iced the drag and the low man tagged, so 5 short-rolled and hit the weak corner” and wants to know what happened. Every one of those words is defined here, in the place where it is used, with a picture.

title: Start here
text:
How it is organized
Four chapters. Chapter 1 is where the game came from: the eras, each bounded by a dated rule change, and the players who defined them. Chapter 2 is how the game is played now, measured. Chapter 3 is the offense and Chapter 4 the defense, each in the order a possession happens, from the break to the late clock, and every offensive action names the coverage built to stop it. The table below is generated from the site’s own navigation, so it cannot disagree with the sidebar.
The sentence at the top of this page needs both Chapter 3 and Chapter 4: the drag and the short roll are offense, the ice, the tag and the low man are the defense’s answers, and the weak corner is court vocabulary, defined in Chapter 3 with the rest of the floor. Every one of those six words now resolves to a written lecture. If a lecture is ever a stub again, its entry in the table below and in the Reference says so, before the click.
Beside the four chapters, the Rules section compares eleven rules across five rule sets (NBA, NCAA men, NCAA women, FIBA, US high school), every cell cited to a rulebook on file or marked as a gap where the text is not public.


Chapters in reading order, from the sidebar.


Chapter
Lectures




1. History and eras
1.1 Origins, 1891 to 1946 · 1.2 The Founding League, 1946 to 1954 · 1.3 The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979 · 1.4 The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001 · 1.5 The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present


2. State of the game
2.1 What Is Different Now · 2.2 The Analytics That Drove It


3. Offense

The Offense and Defense pages list the same lectures by side. The Reference is the database behind the site: every term, one sentence each, with a link to the lecture that teaches it. The search box in the top bar reaches every entry.

title: Start here
text:
How a lecture is written
Each lecture follows the same shape:

Under the title, a short block says which terms are new in this lecture and how many diagrams it has. That block is generated from the database, so it is never out of date with the entries.
Sections are numbered, figures are numbered and captioned, and the prose points at them: “see Section 3”, “Fig. 2”.
Each action or coverage is set out in a numbered card with the same slots every time. For an action: setup, trigger, read, payoff, beaten by. For a coverage: assignment, concedes, requires, beaten by. When a counter is introduced, its card shows what changed from the base action, the way a second model is shown as a diff of the first.
Every term is a link to its entry in the reference, and every entry links back to the lecture.

title: Start here
text:
Reading a diagram
Offense is orange, defense is teal. A numbered circle is an attacker, the small filled dot beside one is the ball, and an X is a defender. A solid arrow is a cut or a run, a squiggle is a dribble, a dashed arrow is a pass, and a short thick bar is a screen; a teal arrow is a defender’s rotation. Diagrams are drawn to NBA dimensions from the rulebook, seen from above with the basket at the bottom; a press or a press break shows the whole floor with the far basket at the top.

section: What is a fact here and what is not
text:
What is a fact here and what is not
Definitions are terminology. They are written straight, because “a pin-down is a screen set facing the baseline” has no source to cite, only common use. Anything empirical carries a source: a number, a trend, a rule change, a claim that a team or a league does something more than it used to. If a claim of that kind has no source it does not appear, or it appears as a stated gap naming what is missing. That line is drawn on purpose, so that a definition can be trusted as vocabulary and a claim can be checked as a claim.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
Eight years separate the first professional season that lasted from the rule that made the professional game watchable. This is the shortest era in the chapter and the one with the clearest ending: the sport acquired a single league, discovered that a league can be won by not playing, and fixed it with a clock.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
1 One league
The BAA began in 1946-47 and was not alone: the National Basketball League already existed. The two merged, and NBA.com’s account of the 1949-50 season states the terms: “the summer of 1949 solidified the professional basketball picture, with the six surviving NBL teams being absorbed into the BAA and the league being renamed the National Basketball Association.”1
That single sentence contains the whole of what this era did structurally. The name the league has used ever since dates from that summer, and the season that followed was the first played under it.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
2 Mikan
The era’s defining player was George Mikan, whose Minneapolis Lakers won the first NBA season: NBA.com’s review of 1949-50 records the season “in which the Minneapolis Lakers emerged as NBA champions” and that “George Mikan led the league” that year.2 He was inducted into the Hall of Fame in its inaugural class, which the Hall’s own list records as “Class of 1959”,3 and Wikipedia’s account of that class adds that he “was the first NBA player to be enshrined.”4






Player


George Mikan, center, Minneapolis Lakers


Standing


Hall of Fame, Class of 1959, inducted as a player in the inaugural class.5 NBA championship, 1949-50, with Minneapolis.6


Second bearing


The induction is confirmed by a second publisher.7 The championship is on one publisher only.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The first player the league wrote rules about rather than for, and the reason the lane was widened while he was still playing.





Player 1: George Mikan: the first player whose presence changed the rules written around him.



The post-up of lecture 3.7 is the action this era was built on, and Mikan is the reason. An offense whose best player stands near the rim with his back to it is an offense that does not need spacing, a three-point line or a ball screen, and for most of this era it did not have any of them.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
section: 3 Bob Cousy and the first fast break
text:
3 Bob Cousy and the first fast break
The other player this lecture cards is the one who made the ball move. Bob Cousy won the Most Valuable Player award once, in 1956-57, which is the single row naming him on the league’s year-by-year list,8 and he entered the Hall of Fame in the Class of 1971.9






Player


Bob Cousy, point guard, Boston Celtics


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 1, in 1956-57.10 Hall of Fame, Class of 1971.11


Second bearing


Both are on one publisher each.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The first guard whose passing was the reason a team ran, and the player the early transition game was built around.





Player 2: Bob Cousy: the ball moving ahead of the defense, twenty years before anyone counted what that was worth.



His award falls just after this era’s boundary, which is worth stating rather than smoothing over: the MVP award did not exist during most of the founding league, and a player whose best years were before an award cannot be measured by it. That is the reason this chapter counts honors rather than compares them across eras.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
4 The clock
The era ends with an arithmetic problem. Nothing in the rules obliged a team with a lead to shoot, so the rational thing to do with a lead was to hold the ball, and teams did. NBA.com’s review of the 1954-55 season records the fix: “it was the adoption of the 24-second clock and an accompanying limit on the number of fouls a team could commit in a quarter.”12 The same page names its author, “Syracuse owner Danny Biasone and his GM, Leo Ferris, came up with the shot clock idea”,13 and quotes the former coach and referee Charlie Eckman: “Danny Biasone saved the NBA with the 24-second rule, make no mistake about that”.14
The clock is the most consequential rule in this chapter, because it created the thing every later lecture assumes: a possession with an end. Pace becomes a number only once possessions are countable, late clock becomes a situation only once there is a clock to be late on, and transition becomes worth measuring only once the alternative has a deadline.
The idea to carry into lecture 1.3 is that the clock did not make the game fast. It made it finite, and the twenty-five years that follow are the sport working out what to do with a possession that has to end.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
A rule can exist for twenty years before anyone uses it properly. That is the story of this era: the three-point line arrived in 1979 and the sport spent two decades treating it as a specialty shot rather than as the thing an offense should be organized around. What the era is remembered for instead is two rookies, one dynasty, and the most physical defense the league has allowed.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
1 The line nobody used
The rule that defines the era arrived complete and was ignored for most of it. What makes this striking is that the arithmetic was available from the first day: a shot worth three is worth taking at a lower success rate than a shot worth two, and the ratio is not subtle. The reason it took twenty years is not that anyone miscalculated but that nobody was counting, which is what lecture 2.2 is about.
The consequence for the vocabulary of this site is that most of Chapter 3 would have looked strange for most of this era. 5-out spacing, the corner three as a designed shot, the kick-out as the main assist: all of them presume the line is worth organizing around.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
3 The physical 1990s and Jordan
The back half of the era is the most physical defense the league has permitted, and the player who defined it is the one who had to play through it.






Player


Michael Jordan, guard, Chicago Bulls


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 5, in 1987-88, 1990-91, 1991-92, 1995-96 and 1997-98.10 Finals Most Valuable Player, 6, which is more rows than any other name on that list.11 Hall of Fame, Class of 2009.12


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The defining player of the era in which defenses were allowed to be at their most physical, and the reason several of the rules about them were rewritten after he stopped.





Player 3: Michael Jordan: six Finals MVP awards, the most on the league’s list.



The defensive rules of this era are the reason isolation was a primary offense rather than a late-clock option. A defense was not permitted to play what would now be called a zone: the illegal-defense rules required defenders to be guarding someone, which meant an attacker who cleared one side of the floor genuinely had it to himself. The isolation of lecture 3.11 is what an offense does when the rules guarantee no help arrives from the weak side.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
4 What changed in 2001
The rules that ended the era did two things. They removed the prohibition on illegal defense, which permitted zone defenses in the professional game for the first time. And they introduced the defensive three-second rule, which prevented a defender from simply standing in the lane to take the rim away, by requiring him to be “actively guarding an opponent within three seconds.”13
Those two changes together produce the game Chapter 3 describes. A defense may now be anywhere, so long as nobody parks in the paint; an offense must therefore create space rather than be handed it; and spacing, the drive and the kick-out become the organizing ideas. That is the subject of lecture 1.5.

title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
Chapter 1 gave dates. This chapter gives measurements, and it is the chapter where this site is most likely to be wrong, because a number is easy to state and hard to check. So every figure below comes from one saved table of league averages, every figure names the season it belongs to, and where a claim is commonly made that this site cannot check, it appears as a gap rather than as a sentence.
One methodological note first, because it changes how the rest of this lecture reads. The table these numbers come from carries two sets of league averages on one page, regular season and playoffs, with the same column names and the same season labels.1 The playoff rows look exactly like the regular-season rows and are different numbers. Everything below is regular season, and the saved extraction labels every row with the table it came from, so that a reader can check which is which.

title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
text:
1 The three-point rate
The clearest change in the modern game is not that teams make more threes. It is that they attempt vastly more of them, as a share of everything they shoot.

League averages per game, regular season. Attempt figures are quoted from the source; the share is computed from the two columns beside it, and tools/check_tables.py recomputes it on every build. {computed='4=2/3%'}

Three things in that table are worth saying plainly.
The line’s first season barely used it. In 1979-80, the season the three-point shot was adopted, teams attempted 2.8 of them a game out of 90.6 shots.2 That is the rule existing and nobody using it, which is the subject of lecture 1.4.
The rate did not rise steadily. It was higher in 1996-97 than in 2004-05. A reader told only that “three-point shooting has increased since the line was introduced” would predict a smooth climb and be wrong about two decades of it.
The table gives five seasons because five is what a reader can hold. Every season from 1979-80 to 2024-25 is in the same source, and drawn as a line the shape says something the five rows cannot (Figure 1): the rise is not one climb but three separate movements, and the middle one is a rule change rather than a change of mind.






Figure 1: Three-point attempts per game, every NBA regular season from 1979-80 to 2024-25. The first decade is flat and near the bottom of the chart. The spike in the middle is the shortened line of 1994-95 to 1996-97 and the drop after it is the line moving back. The climb from the mid 2000s is the one this chapter is about, and it has no flat stretch in it.



The change since 2004-05 is the large one. From 19.7% of shots to 42.2% is the shift that produced the offense of Chapter 3: the spacing, the corner three, the kick-out, the 5-out floor.

Why this lecture opens at 2004-05. The plan for this site anchors Chapter 2 at the 2004-05 rule cluster, on the same criterion Chapter 1 uses: a boundary is a dated rule change. The rule usually named for that season is the elimination of hand-checking, and this site has no source on file for it: NBA.com’s own season review of 2004-05 does not mention a rule change.3 So 2004-05 is used here as the season the measurements pivot around, which the table shows, and not as a rule change, which this site cannot yet source.

title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
text:
2 Pace
Pace is possessions per game, and it is the number that says whether a game is fast.

League averages, regular season.


Season
Pace
Points per game




1979-80
103.1

1996-97

90.9

98.8

The shape of this is not what a viewer usually expects. The modern game is faster than the 1990s and slower than 1979-80: pace fell for two decades and then rose again, and it has not returned to where it was when the three-point line arrived.4
Drawn together across every season, the two numbers make the point more plainly than either makes it alone (Figure 2). They fall together for twenty years and rise together for twenty more, and the rise is not symmetrical: scoring ends well above where it started while pace ends below. The vertical axis of that chart starts at 80 rather than 0, which is stated on the axis itself, because at a zero baseline both lines sit in the top fifth of the picture and the shape this paragraph describes is invisible.






Figure 2: Pace and points per game, every NBA regular season from 1979-80 to 2024-25, on an axis that starts at 80. Both fall to their lows in the shortened 1998-99 season and both rise afterward, but points rise further: the series ends above its 1979-80 value while pace ends below its own. The widening gap between the two lines is what this site means by efficiency.



What has changed more than pace is what a possession is worth. In 1979-80 a game of 103 possessions produced 109 points; in 2024-25 a game of 99 possessions produced 114.5 Scoring is up while pace is down relative to 1979-80, which means the increase is efficiency and not tempo. That is the subject of lecture 2.2.

title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
text:
3 Efficiency and free throws
True shooting percentage is one number that accounts for twos, threes and free throws together. It was .531 in 1979-80, .529 in 2004-05, and .576 in 2024-25.6 Two decades of essentially no change, then a substantial rise.
Free throws moved the other way. Attempts per game were 27.8 in 1979-80, 26.1 in 2004-05, 22.8 in 2014-15 and 21.7 in 2024-25.7 The modern game scores more while shooting fewer free throws, which is worth holding against the common assumption that the increase in scoring is an increase in fouls called.

title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
section: 4 What this lecture does not claim
text:
4 What this lecture does not claim

Shot location is not sourced here. The claim that the mid-range shot has largely disappeared, and that shots have moved to the rim and the arc, is true as far as this site’s authors know and is not on file. The source that publishes shot-location data as a public table is Cleaning the Glass, and its team pages returned HTTP 500 when this site tried to acquire them on 2026-09-21; the league’s own stats pages render their tables with script, and the acquisition tool saved 443 words of page furniture and no data. What would close it: a shot-location table from a source that serves it as HTML, or a saved export.


Positionless lineups and small ball are not sourced here. Both are real and widely described, and neither is a measurement this site has. A count would need lineup data by position, which none of the sources on file carry. What would close it: a public table of lineup composition by season.

Those two gaps are worth as much as the numbers above them. A reader can take every figure in this lecture and check it against the saved table; the two claims in this section are the ones this site would be asking to be believed on, so it does not make them.
The idea to carry into lecture 2.2 is that the numbers here say what changed and not why. The next lecture is about the measurements that changed the decisions: points per possession, the value of a shot by location, and what it means for a shooter to have gravity.

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
New terms introduced (4): Isolation, Mismatch, Motion offense, Read and react. Diagrams: 4.
Nine lectures have named actions. This one is about the offenses that do not call them. A set play tells five players what to do; a conceptual offense tells them what to do if. The instructions are rules attached to events: if the ball is passed, screen away; if a teammate drives at you, cut behind him; if you are denied, back cut. Nobody calls anything, and the actions of lectures 3.2 to 3.9 appear anyway, because the rules produce them.
Section 1 is motion offense, the oldest of these. Section 2 is read and react, the most systematic. Section 3 is the two situations in which an offense deliberately stops moving: isolation and the mismatch. Section 4 is the synthesis this chapter has been building toward: every “beaten by” slot in Chapter 3 is a coverage from Chapter 4, and choosing the action that beats the coverage being shown is what an offense actually does.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
1 Motion offense
Motion offense gives each player a small set of rules about what to do when the ball moves. The classic pair is pass and screen away and fill the spot behind, as in Figure 1. The ball goes from the slot to the wing; the passer screens for someone on the far side rather than cutting toward the ball; the man he screens comes up to fill the spot the passer left. The floor is back in its shape, the ball is on a new side, and the rules apply again.






Figure 1: Motion offense. The ball is passed to the wing; the passer screens away for the far slot; that player fills the spot the passer left. No play was called: each player is following a rule about what to do when the ball moves.









Setup


Four or five players around the perimeter in named spots, one big inside or all five out, and a rule set every player knows.


Trigger


Any pass. The rules are attached to the ball moving.


Read


The passer chooses between the rules his team allows: screen away, cut through, or hold. The screened player reads his own defender with the four reads of lecture 3.5. Every other player fills so the spacing of lecture 3.10 is preserved. If the defense switches everything, the rules produce a mismatch and the offense stops and plays Section 3.


Payoff


Continuous screening and cutting that a defense must guard correctly every time, from an offense that can be run at any tempo and needs no call.


Beaten by


Switching everything, which turns every screen into a non-event and dares the offense to beat a matched-up defense one-on-one; or physical denial that stops the first pass. Lecture 4.5.





Action 1: Motion offense: rules attached to the pass, and the actions appear on their own.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
2 Read and react
Read and react attaches the rules to the drive rather than the pass, and it is the most explicit version of a conceptual offense: each player has a specified reaction to each thing the ball does, learned in layers, as in Figure 2. A baseline drive makes the man behind it circle to the spot it left, the weak-side corner lift to the wing, and the players away from the ball move up a spot. A drive at a teammate makes him cut behind it, which is the 45 cut of lecture 3.7. A pass to the post makes the passer and the nearest teammate cut in opposite directions.






Figure 2: Read and react. The drive is the signal. The player behind the drive fills the spot it left, the weak-side corner lifts, and the man at the top fills behind. Each reaction is a rule triggered by the direction of the drive.









Setup


4-out or 5-out spacing with every player in a named spot, and a rule for each of: a drive at you, a drive away from you, a pass to the post, a dribble at you.


Trigger


A drive, a dribble-at, or a post entry. Not a call.


Read


The driver reads the help exactly as in lecture 3.10. Everyone else executes their reaction without waiting to see whether the drive succeeds, which is what makes the passes available at the instant the help commits.


Payoff


Every drive has three outlets already moving to the right places before the help has finished committing.


Beaten by


A defense that never helps, so no reaction is ever triggered, which requires five defenders who can guard the ball alone; or shrinking the floor so the drives are into single gaps. Lecture 4.4.





Action 2: Read and react: the drive is the signal, and everyone else has a rule for it.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
3 When the offense stops moving
Two situations are worth stopping for.
Isolation clears one side of the floor so one attacker can work alone, as in Figure 3. Everything this chapter has built exists to make two defenders guard one attacker; an isolation is the admission that this particular attacker beats one defender by himself, and the four teammates are there only to keep their own defenders too far away to help. It is the least collective thing an offense does, and it is correct whenever the individual advantage is larger than the advantage a screen would create.






Figure 3: Isolation. The other four attackers have cleared to the far side; the handler has the whole side of the floor and his defender has no help nearer than the nail.









Setup


The handler on a wing or at the top. The other four on the opposite side, spread so their defenders cannot help without leaving a shooter.


Trigger


A favorable individual matchup, or a late shot clock, or an ATO designed for it.


Read


The handler reads whether help comes. No help: beat the man. Help from the nail: the pass back to the top. Help from the weak-side corner: the skip. A second defender arriving on the dribble: the isolation has become a two-on-one and the read is the same as the drive’s.


Payoff


A one-on-one against the defender the offense chose, with no help within a pass.


Beaten by


A defender who stays in front, which is the whole answer; or a defense that sends a second defender early and lives with the pass out. Lecture 4.4.





Action 3: Isolation: clear the side and let one player beat one player.



A mismatch is the same idea created by the defense rather than chosen by the offense. After a switch, a big is guarding a guard or a guard is guarding a big, as in Figure 4. Both are attackable and each has its own route: the guard drives the slower defender, or the big posts the smaller one, which is the post-up and the early seal of lecture 3.7. The defense’s answer is the scram switch of lecture 4.5, which is why the early seal has to be early.






Figure 4: The mismatch. A switch has left a big on the guard and a guard on the big. Two ways to attack it: drive the slower defender, or post the smaller one.









Setup


A switch has just happened. The three players not involved space away to keep help out of the picture.


Trigger


The switch itself. The window is a second or two before the defense fixes it.


Read


Which mismatch is bigger. A guard against a slow big: attack off the dribble before help arrives. A big against a small guard: seal and call for the ball immediately, because a scram switch is coming. If the defense sends help, the man the helper left is open.


Payoff


A drive or a post catch against a defender who cannot guard that player alone.


Beaten by


The scram switch, or switching back at the first dead ball, or a defense whose players are similar enough in size that no switch creates a mismatch at all. Lecture 4.5.





Action 4: The mismatch: the defense made it; take whichever half is bigger, quickly.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
section: 4 The synthesis: read the coverage, pick the action
text:
4 The synthesis: read the coverage, pick the action
Every card in this chapter ends with a “beaten by” slot, and every one of those slots names a coverage from Chapter 4. Reading them the other way round gives the offense’s actual decision procedure, because a coverage that beats one action is usually what makes another one available:

The defense drops on ball screens, conceding the pull-up to protect the rim. Then the pop and the pull-up are open, and the snake gets to them.
The defense plays at the level or hedges, killing the pull-up. Then the slip and the ghost punish the early commitment, and the rocket pass beats the hedge.
The defense traps, taking the ball out of the best player’s hands. Then the short roll and the 4-on-3 are the whole answer.
The defense ices toward the sideline. Then the step-up screen sends the handler baseline instead, and the twist re-screens him back to the middle.
The defense switches everything. Then screens stop mattering and mismatch, early seal and isolation are what is left, which is why switching teams need five players who can guard.
The defense top-locks shooters off screens. Then the back cut is open behind the lock, every time.
The defense helps hard from the weak side. Then the hammer, the kick-out and the skip pass are the punishment.
The defense never helps. Then the drive and the isolation are the offense, because nobody is guarding two players.

This is what a good offense is doing while it looks like it is running a play: showing an action, seeing the coverage, and running the action that beats it. The named actions of lectures 3.4 and 3.6 exist for exactly this reason, which is why each of them was introduced with the coverage it was invented against.
The idea to carry into lecture 3.12 is that all of this assumes a live ball and a set defense. The next lecture is about the possessions that start from neither: out of bounds, after a timeout, against a press, and against a zone.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.2: Early Offense
text:
New terms introduced (10): Delay, Double drag, Drag screen, Dribble handoff, Early offense, Flow offense, Get action, Pistol, Trailer flip, Zoom. Diagrams: 7.
Lecture 3.1 ended with the defense back but back badly: five defenders in the front court, cross-matched, the big still arriving, nobody yet in the stance they will be in ten seconds from now. Early offense is the set of actions built for exactly that state. It is not the break, because the numbers are even. It is not the half court, because the defense is not set. It is the ten seconds in between, and a team that has a plan for those ten seconds gets a good shot before the other team has finished getting organized.
Two things make the window worth attacking. First, the defense has matched up by proximity, not by assignment, so a guard may be standing next to a big and a big next to a guard. Second, the last defender back is usually the big, and the last attacker up is usually the other big. That trailing big is the whole subject of this lecture: he is the one player the defense has not accounted for, and every action below is a way of using him before they do.
This lecture takes the actions in the order a team learns them. Section 1 is the drag screen and the double drag, the trailing big screening the ball. Section 2 is pistol, the guard-to-wing entry. Section 3 is delay and the dribble handoff, the big holding the ball at the top of an empty floor. Section 4 is zoom and get action, the two handoff actions that start from a screen or a pass. Section 5 is what joins them: the trailer flip and flow, the rules that let a team run from one action into the next without a call. Each action is a card with the same five slots, and each card’s last slot names the coverage in Chapter 4 built to stop it.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 1 The trailing big screens the ball
text:
1 The trailing big screens the ball
The drag screen is a ball screen set on the run. The ball-handler is dribbling up one side of the floor; the big is trailing him; instead of running to the block the big runs at the ball-handler’s defender and sets a screen while that defender is still retreating. The screen is set before the defense has decided how to guard screens on this possession, which is the point. See Figure 1.






Figure 1: The drag screen. The trailing big arrives from behind and screens the ball-handler’s defender before his own defender has caught up. The handler comes off toward the middle; the big rolls into an empty lane.









Setup


The ball-handler on one side of the floor, above the arc, dribbling toward the front court with the defense matched but not set. The big trailing the ball by a few steps. The other three attackers filling the corners and the weak-side wing so the lane is empty.


Trigger


The big reaches the ball-handler’s defender before his own defender reaches him.


Read


The ball-handler comes off the screen toward the middle and reads the big’s defender. If that defender is late, the handler turns the corner and drives. If he has arrived and dropped back, the handler has a pull-up, and the big rolls. If he has arrived and stepped up to the ball, the pass to the rolling big is open behind him.


Payoff


A two-on-one against the big’s defender before the help defenders have found their assignments, so the roll or the pop is uncontested.


Beaten by


The big’s defender sprinting rather than jogging back, so he is level with the screen when it is set and can play it as a set defense would. Chapter 4 teaches the coverages; the one built for the drag is to ice it toward the sideline, taught in lecture 4.3, which also covers the drag in lecture 4.2.





Action 1: The drag screen: a ball screen set before the defense has decided how to guard one.



The double drag adds the second big. Two screeners line up one behind the other on the same side, and the ball-handler comes off both. The two screens do two different things: the first screener usually steps out to the arc for a pop, the second rolls to the rim. The defense now has three attackers in the action and only the two screeners’ defenders and the ball defender to handle them, which is what Figure 2 shows.






Figure 2: The double drag. Two trailing bigs screen in a staggered line. The handler comes off both; the first screener pops, the second rolls.









Setup


As the drag, with both bigs trailing on the same side and the two shooters in the corners.


Trigger


The first screener sets his screen; the second screener sets his a step later and a step further along the handler’s path.


Read


The handler comes off both screens toward the middle. The first big pops; the second rolls. The handler reads the second big’s defender: if he stays with the roller, the pop is open; if he steps up to stop the ball, the roll is open; if he splits the difference, the handler shoots.


Payoff


Two bigs in two different places, one at the arc and one at the rim, guarded by defenders who arrived at different times and have not talked.


Beaten by


The two screeners’ defenders sorting out before the screens who will take the pop and who will take the roll, which is the same discipline as any pick-and-roll coverage in lecture 4.3, done on the run.





Action 2: The double drag: one screen becomes two, and one read becomes three.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 2 Pistol: pass ahead, follow the pass
text:
2 Pistol: pass ahead, follow the pass
Pistol starts with a pass rather than a dribble. The point guard, bringing the ball up one side, throws ahead to the wing and then sprints toward the wing himself. The wing dribbles at him and hands the ball back, so the guard receives it moving toward the middle with the wing’s body between him and his defender. The big trails to the top of the key, and the second part of pistol is a ball screen from that big on whichever side the handoff has opened. It is called 21 because the 2 and the 1 run it. See Figure 3.






Figure 3: Pistol. The guard passes ahead to the wing and follows the pass; the wing hands the ball back so the guard receives it moving toward the middle. The big trails at the top for the screen that follows.









Setup


The point guard above the arc on one side, the wing ahead of him at the free-throw line extended, the big trailing to the top, the other two spaced on the weak side.


Trigger


The pass ahead. The guard’s defender relaxes for one step because his man no longer has the ball.


Read


The guard follows the pass. If his defender goes under the handoff, the guard keeps the ball and shoots or turns down toward the trailing big’s screen. If his defender chases over the top, the guard takes the handoff and drives the middle. If the wing’s defender jumps to the guard, the wing keeps the ball and drives baseline, which is the fake handoff.


Payoff


The best ball-handler receives the ball at speed, going toward the middle, with a screen already coming from the trailing big.


Beaten by


Switching the handoff, so the wing’s defender takes the guard and the guard’s defender stays with the wing. Switching is lecture 4.5; the specific answer to a handoff, which is to switch it or to top-lock the receiver so he cannot get to it, is in lecture 4.2.





Action 3: Pistol: the guard gives the ball up to get it back moving.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 3 Delay: the big at the top of an empty floor
text:
3 Delay: the big at the top of an empty floor
Delay gives the ball to the big instead of the guard. The center walks the ball to the top of the key and holds it, and the other four spread to the wings and corners: a 5-out floor with nobody in the paint, taught in lecture 3.10. From there the big has three things he can do, and the defense has to be ready for all three: hand the ball to a guard cutting up to him, screen for a guard who cuts past him without the ball, or reverse the ball to the other side. The most common is the handoff, and Figure 4 shows it.






Figure 4: Delay. The center holds the ball at the top of a 5-out floor. A guard cuts up from the wing to take a handoff; the far corner lifts to keep the spacing. The paint is empty because every defender is guarding a player outside the arc.









Setup


The center at the top with the ball. Two wings, two corners. Every defender is outside the paint because every attacker is.


Trigger


The big’s defender steps back to protect the rim, because that is where he wants to be, and leaves the big alone with the ball at the arc.


Read


One guard cuts up toward the big. The big reads the cutter’s defender. If the defender trails the cutter, the big hands the ball off and the guard drives downhill off his body. If the defender goes under, the big keeps the ball and the guard fades to the arc for a pass. If the defender jumps the handoff early, the big drives himself, into a paint nobody is protecting.


Payoff


A handoff with the whole paint empty behind it, so the driver meets one defender at most.


Beaten by


The big’s defender refusing to drop, guarding the big at the arc and denying the handoff, which puts a rim protector twenty-five feet from the rim; or switching every handoff. Both are in lecture 4.2.





Action 4: Delay: the big holds the ball where his defender does not want to guard him.



The dribble handoff deserves its own card, because it is the unit every action in this lecture is built from. A handoff is a pass and a screen in one motion: the player with the ball dribbles at a teammate, the teammate takes the ball out of his hands, and the first player’s body is in the way of the second player’s defender. It is legal because the handoff is not a screen under the rules; the handler is allowed to stand where he stopped. See Figure 5.






Figure 5: The dribble handoff. The big dribbles from the elbow toward the wing; the guard steps up and takes the ball as they pass. The big’s body screens the guard’s trailing defender, and the guard receives the ball already moving downhill.









Setup


One player with the ball and a live dribble, a teammate within a few steps, the teammate’s defender trailing him or level with him.


Trigger


The handler dribbles at the teammate, and the teammate steps toward the handler so the exchange happens at speed.


Read


The receiver reads his own defender. Trailing: take the handoff and drive off the handler’s hip. Under: refuse the handoff, or take it and shoot, because the defender has gone the long way round. Jumping the handoff: the handler keeps the ball and drives, because the defender has left his man to guard the exchange.


Payoff


The receiver gets the ball with a defender behind him rather than in front of him, which is the same thing a ball screen buys, without a screen the defense can call out.


Beaten by


Switching the exchange, so the receiver’s new defender is already in front of him; or the receiver’s defender going under and the receiver not being a shooter. See lecture 4.2.





Action 5: The dribble handoff: a pass and a screen in one motion, and the unit everything else here is built from.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 4 Zoom and get: the handoff that starts somewhere else
text:
4 Zoom and get: the handoff that starts somewhere else
Zoom puts a screen before the handoff. A shooter starts in the corner; a big sets a pin-down on the shooter’s defender; the shooter runs up off the screen toward the wing; and the ball-handler, who has been dribbling toward the same spot, hands him the ball as he arrives. The shooter has now used two screens in a row, the pin-down and the handler’s body, and is going downhill at full speed while his defender has been hit twice. It is also called Chicago action. The two frames of Figure 6 and Figure 7 show the screen and then the handoff.






Figure 6: Zoom, first frame. The shooter starts in the corner. The big pins down on his defender and he runs up toward the wing; the ball-handler dribbles toward the same spot.









Figure 7: Zoom, second frame. The shooter takes the handoff at the wing at full speed and turns the corner. The pin-down screener has rolled into the lane and the handler has stepped out to the arc.









Setup


The shooter in the corner, a big on the block above him ready to screen, the ball-handler above the arc on the same side, the other two spaced on the weak side.


Trigger


The pin-down. The shooter’s defender is hit by the screen and is now a step behind.


Read


The shooter comes off the pin-down and reads his defender while the handler dribbles at him. Trailing: take the handoff and drive. Going under the pin-down: curl the screen straight to the rim, and the handler passes instead of handing off. Switched, so the big’s defender has jumped out to the shooter: the big who screened rolls into the lane against a smaller defender.


Payoff


A shooter with a live dribble going downhill with his defender two screens behind, or a big rolling against a switched guard.


Beaten by


Top-locking the shooter before the pin-down so he cannot get to the handoff, taught in lecture 4.4, or switching the pin-down and living with the big on the guard.





Action 6: Zoom: a pin-down that flows into a handoff, so the receiver is already moving when he gets the ball.



Get action is the handoff started by a pass. The guard passes to the big at the elbow and follows his pass straight at him. The big turns and hands the ball back as the guard goes by. It is the give and go of lecture 3.7 with a handoff instead of a return pass, and it starts a possession in two seconds from a standstill, which is why teams run it out of a dead ball as often as out of the break. See Figure 8.






Figure 8: Get action. The guard passes to the big at the elbow and runs straight at him; the big hands the ball back as the guard passes and the guard drives off his body.









Setup


The guard with the ball above the arc, the big at the elbow or the slot on the same side, the other three spaced away.


Trigger


The pass to the big. The guard’s defender takes one step off his man, because the man does not have the ball.


Read


The guard runs at the big. Same three reads as the handoff: trailing, take it and drive; under, refuse or shoot; the big’s defender jumping the handoff, the big keeps it and drives.


Payoff


The guard has the ball back, moving, off a big’s body, two seconds after the possession started.


Beaten by


The guard’s defender staying attached through the pass, which denies the handoff and leaves the big with the ball at the elbow, a poor place for most bigs; or the switch. See lecture 4.2.





Action 7: Get action: the give and go with a handoff in place of the return pass.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 5 Flow: how one action becomes the next
text:
5 Flow: how one action becomes the next
None of these actions is meant to be run once and stopped. The trailer flip is the hinge between the break and the half court: the trailing big arrives at the top, takes the reversal pass from the side the ball came up, and swings it to the other side in one motion. Where the drag screen uses the trailing big as a screener, the flip uses him as a passer, and a team usually has a rule for which one he does: screen if the ball is on his side, flip if it is not.
Flow is the name for offense that runs from transition into these actions and then into the half court without a play being called. It is governed by rules rather than a script. The rules are simple and a team’s are its own: which big trails and which rim runs; whether the trailer screens or flips; who fills the corners; what the wing does when the ball comes to him with a big trailing (in most systems, the pistol handoff). What flow buys is time. A called play takes three or four seconds to set up, and in those seconds the defense finishes getting organized. Flow spends those seconds attacking instead.
The idea to carry into lecture 3.3 is that every action here is a version of one thing: getting the ball to a player who is moving, past a defender who is not yet where he wants to be. The half-court offense in the lectures that follow has to manufacture that against a defense that is set, and its main tool for doing so is the ball screen, which the drag has already introduced.

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
text:
New terms introduced (6): Back screen, Cross screen, Flare screen, Pin-down, Rip screen, Stagger. Diagrams: 6.
A ball screen frees the player who already has the ball. An off-ball screen frees the player who is about to get it, and that is a different problem, because the defense is not watching him. A defender guarding a player without the ball stands between his man and the ball, with his head turned to see both, and everything about an off-ball screen is designed around where that defender is looking. A screen he can see coming, he can avoid. A screen set on his blind side, or set while he is turned toward the ball, he cannot.
The six screens in this lecture are the shapes. What distinguishes them is the direction the screen faces and the direction the cutter goes: up toward the perimeter, away along the arc, back toward the rim, across the lane. The named actions of lecture 3.6 are built by combining two or three of these; this lecture is the parts list. Section 1 is the pin-down and the four reads a cutter makes off it, which are the same four reads off every screen here. Section 2 is the flare screen, for a defender who cheats toward the ball. Section 3 is the back screen and the rip screen, both set behind a defender who is watching the ball. Section 4 is the cross screen, the big man’s screen. Section 5 is the stagger, two screens for one cutter.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
section: 1 The pin-down, and the four reads
text:
1 The pin-down, and the four reads
The pin-down is the most common off-ball screen in the sport, and the one every shooter learns first. A shooter starts near the baseline, usually on the block or in the corner. A screener stands above him, facing the baseline, and the shooter runs up off the screen to the wing or the slot for a catch, as in Figure 1. It is also called a down screen, because the screener has come down toward the baseline to set it.






Figure 1: The pin-down. The screener faces the baseline; the shooter starts near the block and runs up off the screen to the wing. His defender, who was between him and the perimeter, has to go around the screen to follow him.



What makes the pin-down teachable is that the cutter has the same four choices off it that he has off every off-ball screen, and the choice is decided by what his defender does:

Curl. The defender chases the cutter over the top of the screen, right behind him. The cutter curls the screen, turning it into a cut toward the rim, and the defender is trailing.
Fade. The defender goes under the screen, between the screener and the rim, to meet the cutter at the wing. The cutter fades the other way, away from the ball toward the corner, and the defender has gone the wrong side of the screen.
Straight cut. The defender is caught on the screen. The cutter comes straight up to the wing and shoots.
Back cut. The defender anticipates and jumps above the screen to deny the catch at the wing. The cutter reverses and goes back door to the rim behind him, the back cut of lecture 3.7.







Setup


The shooter on the block or in the corner, his defender between him and the perimeter. The screener above him, facing the baseline. The ball on the other side of the floor or at the top, in the hands of a passer who can see the wing.


Trigger


The screener sets his feet. The shooter waits until the screen is set, then runs; a cutter who leaves early runs past his own screen.


Read


The shooter reads his defender against the screen: chasing over, curl; going under, fade; caught, straight cut and shoot; jumping above, back cut. The passer reads the same thing one beat later and delivers the ball to the spot the read chose.


Payoff


A shooter catching on the perimeter with his defender behind the screen, or a layup for the cutter who curled or back cut.


Beaten by


Top-locking the shooter: his defender stands above him, between him and the screen, and refuses to let him get to it, conceding the back cut to take away the shot. Taught in lecture 4.4. The other answer is to switch the screen, lecture 4.5.





Action 1: The pin-down: the screen a shooter learns first, and the four reads he makes off every screen after it.



Two names heard for versions of the pin-down have no entry of their own on this site. A wide pin-down is set in the corner or the short corner for a cutter who starts in the corner, so the cut is longer and the catch is at the wing. A double screen is two screeners standing shoulder to shoulder so the cutter’s defender has to go round both; when they are one behind the other instead of side by side, it is the stagger of Section 5. A chin is a back screen set in the slot, on one glossary’s description; another describes it as that back screen followed by a flare for the other slot player, and until the two agree the word has a description here and not a card.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
text:
2 The flare screen
