title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
New terms introduced (13): Crash or get back, Cross-match, Floor balance, Jam the rebounder, Load to the ball, Match up, No layups, Pick-up point, Protect the rim first, Stop the ball, Tandem defense, Transition defense, Transition take foul. Diagrams: 2.
Lecture 3.1 ended by calling every transition advantage a deadline: the numbers last until the defense is back, the empty rim lasts until the big is home, the unguarded trailer lasts until his man arrives. Transition defense is the work of bringing those deadlines forward, and it is unusual among defensive subjects in having almost no scheme to it. There is no coverage to choose. There are three jobs, they come in a fixed order, and the order is the whole lesson.
The order is rim, ball, match up. First the paint is protected, so the shot the offense cannot get is the layup. Then the ball is stopped, so the break slows to a walk. Only then does each defender find a man. Every transition breakdown a coach shows on film is one of these done out of order: a defender who ran to his man while the rim was empty, or a defender who found a body while nobody had the ball.
This lecture takes the three jobs in that order. Section 1 is the rim, Section 2 is the ball, Section 3 is the outnumbered case where both have to be done by two players, and Section 4 is matching up. Section 5 goes back before the shot, to the decisions a defense makes while it is still on offense. Section 6 is the take foul, and what the rule book did to it. Each coverage is set out in a card with four slots, and each card’s last slot names the action from lecture 3.1 that is built to beat it.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
1 Protect the rim first
The first defenders back do not run to a man. They run to the paint. This is the rule behind protect the rim first, and it exists because of how the shots the offense might take rank. A layup is the shot transition produces most and the shot it produces most efficiently, and a defender who runs to a wing while the paint is empty has taken away a corner three and conceded a dunk. Sprinting to the paint takes the layup away, and every other shot is then closed out to from the inside (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Protect the rim first. Three retreating defenders each sprint to the paint before turning to a shooter. The layup is taken away first; the corners are closed out to second, from the inside. This is what the offense’s wide lanes are trying to prevent.



The phrase a coach uses for this is no layups, and it is a rule chosen for a tired player. A defender sprinting back at full speed cannot process where five attackers are. He can process one instruction, and the instruction is: paint. When he gets there he looks up, and only then does he pick a shooter to close out to. The order costs a beat on the perimeter and buys the rim, and the rim is worth more.
Two refinements follow. The first is that defenders load to the ball as they retreat: they shade toward the side the ball is on, so the ball-handler sees bodies in front of him and the far side of the floor is the last thing the defense worries about. The ball scores; the far corner has to be passed to first, and a long cross-court pass is the pass a retreating defense can most afford to allow. The second is that the first big back goes to the rim regardless of who he is guarding. If the opposing big has beaten him down the floor, that is a problem for the match-up in Section 4, not a reason to leave the paint.






Assignment


The first two defenders back sprint to the paint, below the ball, and stop the layup. They close out to shooters only after the paint is protected.


Concedes


The first open three, usually to a wing who stopped at the arc. This is a deliberate trade.


Requires


Effort and one rule. No reading is needed, which is the point.


Beaten by


Running the lanes with a corner fill, which puts shooters exactly where the paint-first defender has to leave them, and the transition three that follows.





Coverage 1: Protect the rim first: the one rule a sprinting player can follow.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
2 Stop the ball
A ball-handler at full speed is a problem for the whole defense, because every defender behind him is back-pedalling and every decision they make is made a second late. Stopping the ball is one defender meeting the ball-handler early enough that he has to slow down, and the value is not in the stop itself but in the seconds it gives the four players behind.
Where the ball is met is the pick-up point, and it is a choice. A defense that picks the ball up at the free-throw line extended in the back court slows the break earlier but leaves that defender further from the paint if he is beaten. A defense that picks it up at the top of the key in the front court gives up the early dribble but keeps its shape. The choice is made by personnel: a team with a rim protector it trusts picks up higher, because a beaten defender is not the end of the possession. A team without one picks up lower and keeps its bodies in the paint.
The defender who takes the ball says so. The one word of communication that transition defense cannot do without is the one that tells the other four that the ball is handled, because the second job is done only once and a defense with two players on the ball has three on the other four.






Assignment


One defender, usually the nearest guard, meets the ball-handler at the pick-up point and turns him, calling it so nobody else comes.


Concedes


The pass. The ball-handler who is stopped will look to move the ball, and the defense is betting that the receivers are covered by Section 1.


Requires


A defender who can slow a guard at speed without fouling, and a pick-up point the whole team agrees on.


Beaten by


The hit-ahead pass, which moves the ball past the pick-up point before the pick-up defender has arrived, and the push by pass rather than by dribble.





Coverage 2: Stop the ball: the second job, done once, called out loud.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
3 Outnumbered
When two defenders face three attackers, or one faces two, the two jobs above have to be done by the same players, and there is a shape for that. It is tandem defense, and the shape is a line, not a row (Figure 2).






Figure 2: Tandem. Two defenders in a line down the middle. The front man steps up to the ball at the free-throw line; when the ball is passed to a wing, the back man takes the receiver and the front man drops to the rim. The middle is never open.



Two defenders side by side leave the middle open, and the ball-handler from lecture 3.1 goes straight down it. Two defenders in a line, one at the free-throw line and one near the rim, present the ball-handler with a defender in front of him and a defender behind that one. The front man stops the ball. When the ball is passed to a wing, the back man goes to the receiver, and the front man drops to the rim to take the back man’s place. Then, if the ball is passed again, they rotate again. The wing pass is conceded; the layup is not, and neither is the drive down the middle.
The tandem holds until help arrives, and it is a delaying action rather than a solution. What it prevents is the outcome the numbers break is designed for: a defender who steps to the ball with nobody behind him.






Assignment


The two defenders form a line in the middle. Front takes the ball; back takes the first pass; front drops to the rim; repeat until the third defender arrives.


Concedes


A wing jumper, and the second pass if it is fast enough.


Requires


Two defenders who know which of them is front, decided by who arrives first and never argued about.


Beaten by


The numbers advantage used patiently: the ball stays in the middle, the wings stay wide, and the ball swings twice faster than the tandem can rotate.





Coverage 3: Tandem: a line, not a row, and the middle is never open.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
4 Match up
Once the rim is protected and the ball is stopped, the break is over and the defense has a possession to defend. It still has no assignments. The third job is matching up, and the rule for it is the one a tired player can follow: take the nearest unguarded attacker, whoever he is, and say his number. A defender who runs past an open attacker to find his own man has left a shooter open for the time it takes to get there, and in transition that time is a shot.
The consequence is that transition match-ups are often wrong by design. A wing ends up on a big; a big ends up on a guard. This is a cross-match, and it is sometimes deliberate: when the offensive big has beaten the defensive big down the floor, the nearest wing takes him at the rim rather than leaving him alone, and the defensive big, arriving last, takes whichever perimeter player is free. The defense has bought a protected rim at the cost of a size mismatch on the perimeter.
What the defense does about that mismatch is the subject of lecture 4.5, where the scram switch is the tool for getting a small defender out of the post and a big one in. For now the rule is simpler: fix the match-up on the next pass, not this one. A defense that tries to sort its assignments while the ball is live has stopped guarding to talk.






Assignment


Each defender takes the nearest unguarded attacker and calls the number. Mismatches are accepted now and fixed on the next pass.


Concedes


A mismatch somewhere on the floor, usually a small guard on a big or a big on a guard.


Requires


Talk. Five players who each say one number, once.


Beaten by


An offense that finds the mismatch before the defense fixes it: the early seal by a big on a small defender, or a guard attacking a big on the perimeter before the scram switch can happen.





Coverage 4: Match up: the third job, and the one where being wrong is allowed.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
5 Before the shot goes up
Most of transition defense is decided before the possession changes, while the team is still on offense. The question is who goes to the offensive glass and who retreats, and it is the mirror of the crash or get back decision from lecture 3.1. Every player sent to the glass is a rebound the team might win and a defender it will not have. The rule most teams adopt is floor balance: one or two designated players, usually the guards and usually the ones furthest from the rim when the shot goes up, retreat as the shot is released, whatever happens to it. They are the first defenders back in Section 1, and they are back because they never went.
One glossary names a rule that sits between the two: tag up, in which every offensive player, as the shot goes up, matches up with the defender boxing him out and stays between that player and the basket, so that the team still contests the offensive rebound and is already matched when the rebound is lost. It is described by one publisher only, so under this site’s rule it has no entry until a second names it (plan/PLAN.md, section 8.4).
The other thing a defense can do before the break starts is make it start late. Jamming the rebounder is the nearest player staying on the defensive rebounder as he lands, with a hand up in the passing lane, and the next player denying the outlet man on the sideline. The outlet is thrown a second late, or thrown to the middle, or not thrown. A break that starts a second late meets the defense from Section 1 already in the paint, and the whole of lecture 3.1’s first three seconds have been taken away before the first dribble.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
section: 6 The take foul, and what the rule book did to it
text:
6 The take foul, and what the rule book did to it
For a long time there was a fourth job available, cheaper than the other three. If the break could not be stopped, a defender could foul the ball-handler early, before the numbers advantage was used, and trade the breakaway for two free throws and a set defense behind them. This is the transition take foul. Teams did it because they judged two free throws, which can be missed, a better outcome than an uncontested layup, and because the foul bought the time to get all five defenders back for whatever followed.
The NBA changed the trade. Beginning with the 2022-23 season, the penalty is listed in two bullets: “The offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “The offensive team will retain possession of the ball.”1 The foul now costs the defense a free throw and the possession it was trying to save, so the trade it was making no longer exists. The card below shows the coverage as a diff of itself, before and after, in the way a second model is shown as a change to the first.






Assignment


A defender fouls the ball-handler early in the break, before the numbers advantage is used.


Concedes


Two free throws, then a set defense. One free throw, taken by the best shooter on the floor, and the offense keeps the ball.


Requires


Nothing but the decision. A reason to give up a free throw and the ball to prevent one shot, which is hard to find.


Beaten by


Nothing on the floor. The rule.





Coverage 5: The take foul before and after 2022-23: the same action, a different trade.



The idea to carry into lecture 4.2 is that the three jobs do not end when the ball is stopped. The defense that has protected the rim, stopped the ball and matched up is back, but it is back badly: cross-matched, with its big still arriving and its assignments improvised. Early offense is the offense’s attack on exactly that state, and it starts with the one player the defense in Section 4 could not account for, the trailer stepping into a ball screen. The next lecture is about guarding him.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
Footnotes


NBA, “NBA Board of Governors approves heightened penalty for ‘transition take foul’”, NBA.com, 13 July 2022, https://www.nba.com/news/nba-board-of-governors-approves-heightened-penalty-for-transition-take-foul, retrieved 2026-09-17. Verbatim: “Beginning with the 2022-23 NBA season”, the penalty is listed in two bullets, “The offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “The offensive team will retain possession of the ball.” Saved as nba-2022-take-foul in the source registry, 2026-09-21. No claim is made here about how often the old trade paid off; that would need free-throw and breakaway conversion rates with a source, and none is cited.↩︎

title: Offense
text:
The offense’s job in one sentence: get two defenders to guard one player, then pass to the one nobody is guarding. Every phase below is a different way to force that.


Offense lectures in reading order.


Lecture
What it teaches




2.2 The Analytics That Drove It
Points per possession as the currency, the arithmetic of the corner three, gravity, and how much of the modern game follows from one division.


3.1 Transition Offense
The break in the order it unfolds: the outlet and push, the lanes and rim run, the numbers read, the trailer and secondary break, how transition is counted.


3.2 Early Offense
The first action against a defense that is back but not organized: the drag and double drag, pistol, delay and the handoff, zoom, get action, and the flow that joins them.


3.3 On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
The screen, the pick-and-roll, roll, pop, short roll, the step-up screen, the snake dribble, the lob and the 4-on-3 behind a trap.


3.4 On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
Ram, Spain, ghost, slip and twist: the ball-screen actions that exist because the coverages got good at guarding the plain pick-and-roll, and the names heard for them that are not yet entries.


3.5 Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
Pin-down, flare, back screen, rip, cross screen, stagger: the six shapes a screen away from the ball can take, and the four reads a cutter makes off any of them.


3.6 Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
Elevator, Hammer, Floppy, Loop and Wedge: the named actions built from the six screen shapes, each taken apart into its parts, plus the names heard that have no entry yet.


3.7 Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
What a player without the ball does when nobody screens for him: the post-up and the early seal, the cuts that punish a defender’s eyes (45, back, flash, stampede), the cuts that use a body (UCLA, Iverson), give and go, high-low, and the lift and pinch post that keep the floor spaced.


3.8 Sets and Systems
The alignment a team starts from and the script it runs: Horns, Zipper, the set play as a concept, and the named sets and plays heard that have no entry yet.


3.9 Continuity and Read-Based Systems
Offenses that do not end: Princeton, Flex and dribble drive motion, each a whole system rather than an action, and what distinguishes a continuity from a set play.


3.10 Spacing and Roles
The floor and its spots, the alignments, the gap and why its width decides everything, the drive, kick-out and skip pass, and the five roles as they are actually played now.


3.11 Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
Offense run from rules rather than a script: motion, read and react, isolation and the mismatch, and the synthesis of every beaten-by slot in this chapter.


3.12 Special Situations, Offense
Possessions that do not start with a live ball or a set defense: BLOB and SLOB, the box and stack sets they run from, the ATO, the press break and zone offense.


3.13 Late Clock, Offense
When the clock, not the defense, is the constraint: the late-clock possession and the 2-for-1.



Terms by family: transition offense · early offense · on-ball screens · off-ball screens · cuts and actions · sets and systems.

title: Analytics and trends
text:
The measurements behind the choices, and what has changed recently. Every claim here carries a source.
All families · 3 terms · 1 full, 1 partial, 1 short

Corner three
A three-point attempt from the corner, where the line is closest to the rim.
Why it is run. The three-point line is an arc cut off by the sidelines, so a corner three is taken from 22 feet rather than 23 feet 9 inches and is worth the same three points; it is also the shot the weak-side helper has to leave to guard.
What beats it. A defense that never leaves the corner, which concedes the drive; or an X-out rotation that covers the corner with a different defender than the one who helped.
offense · General · full · Taught in lecture 2.2 · See also Corner, Spacing


Gravity
The pull a shooter exerts on defenders who will not leave him, which opens space for teammates.
Why it is run. A defender who will not leave a shooter is a defender who is not helping, so a shooter’s value shows up in shots other players take; it is why five players on the arc create nothing unless their defenders have to respect them.
offense · General · partial · Taught in lecture 2.2 · See also Spacing, Corner three


Points per possession
Also: PPP, efficiency
Points scored divided by possessions used; the standard measure of how good a shot, a play type or a lineup is.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Pace

title: Cuts and actions
text:
The movements that are not screens: handoffs, cuts, seals, drives and the passes that follow.
All families · 19 terms · 16 full, 0 partial, 3 short

45 cut
A perimeter player cutting to the rim at a 45-degree angle when his defender’s eyes leave him to help on a drive.

Why it is run. A defender whose head turns to a drive cannot see his own man; the cut to the rim at 45 degrees behind him is the drop-off the drive did not need to reach the rim to create.
What beats it. Helping with the eyes and not the feet, or a stunt at the drive that keeps the defender close enough to recover.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Drive, Lift


Back cut
Also: backdoor
A cut behind an overplaying defender to the rim.

Why it is run. A defender who denies the pass has his weight toward the ball and his back to the rim; the cut behind him is a layup he chose to allow.
What beats it. Denying with the ball-side foot and hand only and staying half a step lower than the man, or top-locking only with help under the rim.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Top-lock


Dribble handoff
Also: DHO, handoff
The ball-handler dribbles toward a teammate and hands the ball off, screening the receiver’s defender in the same motion.

Why it is run. A handoff gets the receiver the ball with a defender behind him instead of in front of him, which is what a ball screen buys, without a screen the defense can call out.
What beats it. Switching the exchange so the receiver’s new defender is already in front, or going under against a receiver who cannot shoot.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Zoom, Pistol, Get action


Drive
Also: penetration
Dribbling past a defender toward the rim to score or to force help and pass.

Why it is run. Beating a man into the gap forces a second defender to commit, which is what a ball screen buys without needing a screen; from that moment the driver is looking at the man the helper left, not at the rim.
What beats it. Guarding the drive with one defender, a stunt that fakes help and recovers, or a wall in the middle that concedes the pull-up.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Gap, Kick-out


Early seal
A big pinning a smaller defender under the rim the instant a switch happens, before the defense can fix it.

Why it is run. A switch puts a small defender on the big for one or two seconds; pinning him under the rim before help or a switch-back arrives turns that instant into a layup.
What beats it. The scram switch, a third defender taking the big before the entry pass while the small defender rotates out.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Switch, Scram switch, Post-up


Flash
A quick cut into an open spot in the defense, usually across the lane toward the ball, to catch where nobody is guarding.

Why it is run. A defense that shifts toward the ball leaves a spot, usually the free-throw line, and the weak-side player who cuts into it catches facing the basket in the middle of the defense.
What beats it. A defender who bumps the flasher crossing the lane and keeps a body between him and the ball; in a zone, the middle defender whose spot it is.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Pinch post, Zone offense


Get action
Also: get
A guard passes to a big and immediately follows the pass to take a handoff back, a two-man action that starts a possession.

Why it is run. A pass and a return handoff start a possession in two seconds from a standstill, with the guard receiving the ball moving off a big’s body.
What beats it. The guard’s defender staying attached through the pass, which denies the handoff and leaves the big holding the ball at the elbow.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Dribble handoff, Pistol


Give and go
Pass to a teammate, cut to the rim, and get the ball back.

Why it is run. A defender relaxes for one step when his man gives up the ball, and one step is enough for the cut to the rim and the return pass.
What beats it. Jumping to the ball on the pass, so the defender is between his man and the rim before the cut starts.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Back cut, Get action


High-low
Also: hi-lo
Two bigs, one at the high post and one at the low post; the high one catches and feeds the low one, who has sealed his man.

Why it is run. The low post’s seal holds a fronting defender where he is while the pass comes from the high post above, where the fronting defender cannot reach it.
What beats it. The low defender playing behind rather than fronting so there is no seal to hold, or the weak-side low man arriving on the catch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Post-up, Early seal, Pinch post


Iverson cut
Also: Piston cut
A cut from one wing to the other across two screens set at the elbows, to catch on the move.

Why it is run. Wing to wing over two bigs at the elbows puts two bodies between the cutter and his defender and delivers the catch on the move, with the whole side of the floor ahead.
What beats it. Going under both bigs along the free-throw line to meet the cutter at the far wing, conceding the curl, or switching at the second elbow.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Stagger, Horns


Kick-out
Also: drive and kick
A pass from a driver to a perimeter shooter whose defender helped on the drive.

Why it is run. The pass to the shooter whose defender helped is the shot the drive was for; with a shooter in each corner the help has to come from one of them.
What beats it. A closeout short enough to contest the shot without giving up the drive, or an X-out rotation that covers the corner with a different defender.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Drive, Skip pass


Lift
A corner player moving up to the wing as the ball is driven baseline, to give the driver a kick-out.
offense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Drive, Corner


Lob
Also: alley-oop
A pass thrown above the rim for a player to catch and finish in the air.
offense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Dunker spot, Roll


Pinch post
A big catching at the elbow facing the ball, from where he can hand off, shoot or pass to a cutter.
offense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Elbow, Dribble handoff


Post-up
An offensive player establishing position near the block with his back to the basket to receive an entry pass.

Why it is run. Position on the block with the defender sealed behind puts the ball a few feet from the rim and makes every move a guess for the defender; it is also where a size mismatch is worth most.
What beats it. Fronting the post with weak-side help behind so the lob is contested, or a dig from the nearest guard on the catch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Block, Early seal, Mismatch


Skip pass
A pass across the floor that skips the nearest player, usually to punish a defense loaded to the ball.

Why it is run. A defense shifted to one side has to recover across the whole floor, and the closeout from the paint to the far corner is the longest in the game.
What beats it. Two defenders splitting the difference on the weak side so neither closeout is long, at the cost of leaving the strong-side help thin.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Weak side, Kick-out


Stampede cut
Catching the ball already at full speed to blow past a slower defender closing out.

Why it is run. A closeout from the paint has fifteen feet to cover; a receiver already moving to the rim at the catch makes those feet impossible and beats the closeout before it arrives.
What beats it. A short, choppy closeout that never overruns the receiver, conceding the pull-up to stop the drive.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Switch, Closeout


UCLA cut
Also: UCLA screen
A pass from the top to the wing, then a cut to the ball-side block off a back screen set at the elbow.

Why it is run. The pass to the wing turns the passer’s defender’s head, and the big at the elbow is a back screen whether or not one was called, so the guard arrives on the block with his defender behind him.
What beats it. Jumping to the ball side of the big before the cut and riding the cutter to the block, or a switch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.7 · See also Back screen, Post-up


Zoom
Also: Chicago action
A pin-down screen that flows straight into a dribble handoff, so the receiver arrives at the handoff already moving.

Why it is run. A shooter who has used a pin-down and then a handoff has beaten his defender twice in a row and gets the ball going downhill at full speed.
What beats it. Top-locking the shooter before the pin-down so he never reaches the handoff, or switching the pin-down.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Pin-down, Dribble handoff

title: Help and rotations
text:
What the other three defenders do when the first two are beaten.
All families · 13 terms · 13 full, 0 partial, 0 short

Closeout
A defender sprinting from help back to a shooter and slowing down as he arrives, to contest without being driven past.

Why it is run. A shooter who sees a defender arriving out of control does not shoot, he drives, so the sprint back must end in short steps and a high hand or it has traded an open three for an open layup.
What beats it. The stampede, the drive into a closeout that arrives out of control; and a release quick enough that the sprint does not matter.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Stampede cut, Kick-out


Dig
A perimeter defender reaching in at a post player or a driver without leaving his man entirely.

Why it is run. A hand down at the post from the perimeter makes the post player protect the ball for the half-second his move needed, without leaving a shooter, because the digger’s body never leaves his man.
What beats it. The post player who passes out of the dig at once to the man it came from; and a shooter who relocates while his defender’s hand is down.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Stunt, Nail


Help side
The weak-side defenders’ positioning, sagged toward the lane to help on drives while still able to recover to shooters.

Why it is run. Two passes away is far enough that a defender can stand in the lane and still recover to his man in the time the pass takes, so the weak side is where a defense keeps its spare bodies.
What beats it. The skip pass, thrown over the sagged defenders to the far wing before they can recover; and shooters good enough that the recovery is too late.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Weak side, Nail, Low man


Low man
The weak-side defender nearest the baseline, whose job is to rotate to the rim on a drive or a roll.

Why it is run. Someone has to meet the roller and the driver at the rim, and the weak-side defender nearest the baseline is the one whose man is furthest from the ball and whose leaving costs the least.
What beats it. The kick-out to the weak corner he left; the skip pass over him; the hammer, which screens him on his way back.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Tag, X-out, Corner


Pack line
Also: pack-line defense
A man-to-man scheme in which the on-ball defender pressures and the other four stay inside an imaginary line a step or two inside the arc, giving up the perimeter shot to close the drive.

Why it is run. Four defenders inside a line a step inside the arc make every drive meet two bodies, and the shot they give up is a contested one from a closeout, which the scheme judges the better trade.
What beats it. Shooters who make the contested three; drive-and-kick offense that moves the ball faster than four defenders close out from the line.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Help side, Nail, Low man


Peel switch
A beaten on-ball defender peels off to the nearest open attacker while a helper takes the driver.

Why it is run. Once a defender is beaten and a helper has stepped up, the beaten man is the one player out of the play, so he fills the hole the help left rather than chasing a ball he cannot reach.
What beats it. The kick-out thrown before the peel arrives; a helper who steps up late, so the driver has the layup before anyone has switched.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.5 · See also Switch, Closeout


Scram switch
Also: kick-out switch
An off-ball switch that gets a small defender out of a post mismatch by sending a bigger defender in to take it.

Why it is run. A switching defense creates mismatches on purpose and cannot live with a small on a big in the post, so the weak-side big trades in before the entry pass and the mismatch is gone before it is used.
What beats it. The early seal and a quick entry, which get the ball into the post before the scram; the skip pass to the man the big left as he crosses.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.5 · See also Switch, Early seal, Mismatch


Stunt
A fake at the ball from the nail to slow a driver, then recovering.

Why it is run. A hard step at the driver from the nail makes him see a body that never comes, and a driver who slows for it has handed the beaten defender the time to recover, at no cost to the stunter’s own man.
What beats it. The driver who does not slow; and the pass to the stunter’s man the moment his step is seen.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Dig, Nail


Tag
Also: tagged
The low man stepping into the lane to bump the roller, then recovering to his shooter.

Why it is run. Every coverage leaves the roller unguarded for a beat between the two defenders in the screen, and a bump from the low man buys the big that beat without giving up the corner for longer than one pass takes.
What beats it. The short roll, which gives the roller the ball during the tag; the kick-out if the tag holds too long; the Spain back screen on the tagger.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Low man, Roll


The hit
A late-clock gamble where a second defender sprints at the ball unprompted to force a rushed decision.
Why it is run. With the shot clock nearly out, a second defender sprinting at the ball forces a decision the handler has no time to make, and the man the hitter left is worth less than the possession the clock is about to end.
What beats it. The pass to the man the hitter left, made before the trap arrives; the handler who sees the clock and the open man at once.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Blitz, Late clock


Top-lock
A defender standing above a shooter to deny the pin-down and force him backdoor toward the rim protector.

Why it is run. Standing above a shooter and refusing him the path to his pin-down leaves him only the backdoor cut, which is a cut into the rim protector, so the screen the play was built on is never used.
What beats it. The back-cut for a layup when the big is late; the screener who slips out to the arc while the top-locker’s back is turned.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Pin-down, Back cut


Verticality
A rim protector contesting straight up with arms raised, which is legal contact even inside the restricted area.
Why it is run. A rim protector who jumps straight up inside his own space has committed no foul whatever the shooter does, so the rule lets a big contest at the rim without swatting at the ball.
What beats it. The pump fake that draws the arms down; the shooter who jumps into the big before he is set, so the contact is his to draw.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Restricted area


X-out
Two weak-side defenders swapping men on a kick-out, one down to the corner and one up to the wing, crossing paths.

Why it is run. When the low man is under the rim and the ball goes to his corner, the wing defender is closer to the corner than he is, so each closes out to the nearer man and the paths cross.
What beats it. The extra pass, corner to wing, before the low man arrives; the skip pass from the other side that puts the defense a rotation behind.
defense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Low man, Tag

title: Late clock and endgame
text:
What changes when the clock, not the defense, is the constraint.
All families · 4 terms · 3 full, 1 partial, 0 short

2-for-1
Shooting quickly at the end of a period so the offense gets two possessions to the opponent’s one.

Why it is run. Shooting by about twenty-eight seconds at the end of a period gives the offense two possessions to the opponent’s one, worth roughly a point at average efficiency.
What beats it. The opponent holding the ball on the possession in between so the extra one is a heave; and a shot rushed so badly that it costs more than the extra possession gains.
offense · Late clock · full · Taught in lecture 3.13 · See also Late clock, Pace


Foul game
Also: fouling up three, intentional fouls
Deliberately fouling late in a game to stop the clock and trade free throws for possessions.
Why it is run. A trailing team needs possessions and the clock is taking them away, so it buys one with a foul and pays in free throws that can be missed; the trade is bad and made only when the alternative is certain.
What beats it. Free throws made; the offense getting the ball to its best shooter before the foul comes.
defense · Late clock · full · Taught in lecture 4.9 · See also Transition take foul


Hack-a
Also: Hack-a-Shaq
Fouling a poor free-throw shooter away from the ball to give the offense two free throws instead of a possession.
Why it is run. Two free throws by a player who misses most of them are worth less than one ordinary possession, so fouling him away from the ball holds the offense below a point per trip without guarding it.
What beats it. Taking the target off the floor, the target making his free throws, and the away-from-the-play rule, which inside its window makes the foul one free throw by any player and the ball back.
defense · Late clock · full · Taught in lecture 4.9 · See also Foul game


Late clock
The last seconds of the shot clock, when the offense has to get a shot up and the defense can gamble.
Why it is run. Under about seven seconds the constraint is the clock, not the defense, so the order of preference inverts: a contested two that is taken beats a better shot that is not, the actions shrink to one read, and the offensive rebound is worth more.
offense / defense · Late clock · partial · Taught in lecture 3.13 · See also The hit, Isolation

title: On-ball screens
text:
Screens for the player with the ball, and the family that grew out of the pick-and-roll.
All families · 14 terms · 12 full, 0 partial, 2 short

Double drag
Two drag screens in a row from two trailing bigs; typically the first pops and the second rolls.

Why it is run. Two screens put three attackers in one action against three defenders who arrived at different times; the first pops and the second rolls, so one defender cannot cover both.
What beats it. The two screeners’ defenders agreeing before the screens who has the pop and who has the roll, and the ball defender chasing over both.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Drag screen, Pop, Roll


Drag screen
Also: drag
A ball screen set by a trailing big while the defense is still retreating.

Why it is run. A ball screen set while the screener’s defender is still retreating is a screen the defense has not yet decided how to guard; it buys a two-on-one before the help has assignments.
What beats it. The screener’s defender sprinting back level with the screen, then icing it to the sideline.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Double drag, Trailer, Early offense


Ghost screen
The screener runs at the handler’s defender as if to screen, makes no contact and slips out to the arc.

Why it is run. A screener who threatens the screen and runs to the arc without contact leaves the handler’s defender behind a screen that never came and the screener’s defender guarding a roll that never comes.
What beats it. Guarding the screen only once it is set, or a switch called early enough that the ghost is picked up at the arc.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.4 · See also Slip, Pop


Pick-and-roll
Also: PnR, ball screen
An on-ball screen after which the screener rolls to the rim, forcing two defenders to handle two threats.

Why it is run. A screen for the ball puts the handler’s defender behind the ball and forces the screener’s defender to help; the roller behind him is then unguarded. Two defenders, two threats, one of them late.
What beats it. A coverage that decides in advance which threat to concede; the drop gives up the mid-range pull-up to take away the roll and the drive.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Roll, Pop, Short roll, Drop coverage


Pop
Also: pick-and-pop
The screener stepping out to the perimeter for a shot after the screen rather than rolling.

Why it is run. A screener who can shoot punishes the drop, because the dropping defender is at the free-throw line guarding a drive while his man shoots a three above him.
What beats it. Keeping the screener’s defender attached, by switching the screen or playing it at the level.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Roll, Pick-and-roll


Ram
Also: ram screen, screen-the-screener
A pin-down for the big just before he sets the ball screen, so his defender arrives late to the pick-and-roll.

Why it is run. A pin-down on the screener’s defender just before the ball screen makes that defender a step late, so whatever coverage the defense planned is played by a man who is still running.
What beats it. Switching the pin-down so the nearest defender guards the ball screen, or the screener’s defender going under the pin-down and beating the screener to the spot.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.4 · See also Pin-down, Pick-and-roll


Roll
The screener turning and running to the rim after the screen.
offense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Pick-and-roll, Short roll, Pop


Screen
Also: pick
A stationary player placing his body in a defender’s path to free a teammate.
offense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Pick-and-roll, Pin-down


Short roll
Also: short-rolled
The screener rolling only to the free-throw line to catch and make a play against a defense that has trapped or switched.

Why it is run. Against a trap the screener stops at the free-throw line, catches the pass out, and has three teammates against three defenders, with the weak-side low man unable to guard two of them.
What beats it. A trap fast enough to make the pass out a turnover, or an X-out rotation that covers two spots with one man for the two seconds the trap needs to recover.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Roll, Blitz, 4-on-3


Slip
The screener cutting to the rim before the screen is set, punishing a defense that jumped early to the screen.

Why it is run. Two defenders who step up to a screen before it is set are two defenders above the play; the screener who cuts to the rim instead is behind both of them.
What beats it. The screener’s defender staying between him and the rim until the screen is actually set, or a low man who tags the slip early.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.4 · See also Ghost screen, Roll


Snake dribble
After a ball screen, the handler cuts back across in front of the trailing defender, keeping him on his back and playing two-on-one with the dropping big.

Why it is run. Cutting back across the chasing defender keeps him on the handler’s back and leaves the handler alone against the dropping big while the roller comes down the far side.
What beats it. The chaser going under the screen so there is nobody to snake in front of, or the big playing at the level so there is no room to change direction.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Drop coverage, Pick-and-roll


Spain pick-and-roll
Also: stack pick-and-roll
A pick-and-roll with a third player back-screening the roller’s defender and then popping to the arc.

Why it is run. A back screen on the roller’s defender frees the roller to the rim, and the back-screener then pops to the arc, so the drop coverage loses the defender it depends on and gains a shooter to guard.
What beats it. Switching the back screen so the shooter’s defender takes the roller, or the ball defender going under the first screen so the handler never turns the corner.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.4 · See also Pick-and-roll, Back screen


Step-up screen
A ball screen set with the screener’s back to the baseline, sending the handler toward the baseline rather than the middle.

Why it is run. A screen set from below sends the handler toward the baseline, where a coverage built to force everything to the sideline has no rule for him.
What beats it. Switching it, or a big who plays it at the level and turns the handler back toward the middle.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Ice, Pick-and-roll


Twist
Also: re-screen
A second ball screen set from the other side right after the first, so the handler changes direction on the defense.

Why it is run. A second screen on the handler’s other shoulder gives the defense the same problem in the opposite direction while both defenders are still leaning toward the first.
What beats it. The ball defender going under the second screen and conceding the pull-up, or a big who plays both screens at the level and never leans.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.4 · See also Pick-and-roll

title: Presses
text:
Full-court and three-quarter-court pressure, and what it is built to force.
All families · 1 terms · 1 full, 0 partial, 0 short

1-2-1-1 press
Also: diamond press
A full-court zone press shaped like a diamond with a point on the inbounder, built to trap the first pass the moment it is caught.

Why it is run. A trap on the very first catch, with the inbounder still out of bounds and no dribble taken, wins the ball ninety feet from the offense’s basket if the receiver panics, and every pass out of it has to travel the whole floor.
What beats it. The press break: the immediate reversal away from the trap, the outlet to the middle before it closes, and the pass ahead into a four-on-three.
defense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 4.7 · See also Press, Press break

The equipment appendix (ring and backboard sizes) is a separate PDF, also on file. FIBA states its dimensions in metres; the court module converts them to feet and says so.

title: Rules: FIBA
text:
The floor and spacing

Restricted area
The half-circle in front of the rim inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge. Entry.
A no-charge semi-circle of 1.30 m radius from the point beneath the center of the basket; FIBA uses the words “restricted area” for the lane itself. Art. 2.5.7

Verbatim: “A semi-circle line with the radius of 1.30 m measured from the point on the court beneath the exact centre of the basket to the outer edge of the semi-circle.” FIBA’s own “restricted areas” are the lanes: “The restricted areas shall be the rectangular areas marked on the court limited by the endlines, the extended free-throw lines and the lines which originate at the endlines”.

title: Rules: FIBA
text:
Transition defense

Transition take foul
A deliberate foul on the ball early in a break to stop the play before the numbers advantage can be used. Entry.
An unsportsmanlike foul, until the offensive player starts the act of shooting; free throws plus a frontcourt throw-in. Art. 37.1.1; Art. 37.2.2

Verbatim, among the definitions of an unsportsmanlike foul: “An unnecessary contact caused by the defensive player in order to stop the pro-gress of the offensive team in transition. This applies until the offensive player starts the act of shooting.” Penalty, verbatim: “Free throw(s) shall be awarded to the player who was fouled, followed by:” then “A throw-in from the throw-in line in the team’s frontcourt, opposite the scorer’s table.”

title: Rules: FIBA
text:
Rules and regulations

Backcourt count
The time a team has to bring the ball across the midcourt line; the count a press is built to run out. Entry.
8 seconds. Art. 28.1.1

Verbatim: “that team must cause the ball to go into its frontcourt within 8 seconds.”



Court dimensions
The length and width of the playing court. Entry.
28 m by 15 m, inside the boundary line. Art. 2.1

Verbatim: “The court shall have a flat, hard surface free from obstructions (Diagram 1) with dimensions of 28 m in length by 15 m in width measured from the inner edge of the boundary line.”



Defensive three seconds
The NBA rule that a defender in the lane must be guarding someone within three seconds; the reason a rim protector cannot simply stand under the basket. Entry.
No such rule; checked against Official Basketball Rules 2024, v1.0a.

Art. 26 restricts the offensive player only, verbatim: “A player shall not remain in the opponents’ restricted area for more than 3 conse-cutive seconds while the team is in control of a live ball in the frontcourt and the game clock is running.” The text was searched for a defensive count and none appears.



Free-throw lane
How wide the painted lane is; the number behind the paint, the blocks and the elbows. Entry.
4.90 m, the lane lines’ outer edges 2.45 m either side of the midpoint of the endline. Art. 2.5.3

Verbatim: “the lines which originate at the endlines, their outer edges being 2.45 m from the mid-point of the endlines and terminating at the outer edge of the extended free-throw lines.” The width is this site’s arithmetic, twice 2.45 m.



Free-throw line
How far the free-throw line is from the backboard; it fixes the nail and the elbows. Entry.
5.80 m from the inner edge of the endline. Art. 2.5.3

Verbatim: “The free-throw line shall be marked parallel to each endline. It shall have its furthest edge 5.80 m from the inner edge of the endline and shall be 3.60 m long.”



Goaltending
Touching a shot on its way down, or off the backboard, while it can still score; the rule that limits what a rim protector may do. Entry.
Touching a shot while it is completely above ring level and on its downward flight, or after it has touched the backboard. Art. 31.2.1

Verbatim: “Goaltending occurs during a shot for a goal when a player touches the ball while it is completely above the level of the ring and:” then “It is on its downward flight to the basket, or” and “After it has touched the backboard.”



Length of the game
How long a game is and how it is divided; the one rule every other clock hangs on. Entry.
Four quarters of 10 minutes. Art. 8.1

Verbatim: “The game shall consist of 4 quarters of 10 minutes each.”



Shot clock
The time a team has to attempt a shot that reaches the ring; the number that sets the pace of every possession. Entry.
24 seconds; 14 seconds after an offensive rebound or on certain frontcourt throw-ins. Art. 29.1.1; Art. 29.2

Verbatim: “that team must attempt a shot for a goal within 24 seconds.” and, on the frontcourt reset, “If 14 seconds or more are displayed on the shot clock at the time when the game was stopped, the shot clock shall not be reset but shall continue from the time it was stopped.”



Three-point line
How far the arc is from the basket, and how far the corner line is from the sideline; the geometry every spacing decision in Chapter 3 rests on. Entry.
An arc of 6.75 m from the point beneath the center of the basket, meeting lines 0.90 m from the sidelines. Art. 2.5.4

Verbatim: “An arc of radius 6.75 m measured from the point on the court beneath the exact centre of the opponents’ basket to the outer edge of the arc.” and “The 2 parallel lines extending from and perpendicular to the endline, with the outer edge 0.90 m from the inner edge of the sidelines.”

title: Rules: NCAA men
text:
The floor and spacing

Restricted area
The half-circle in front of the rim inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge. Entry.
A semicircle of 4-foot radius from the center of the basket, extended straight to the front face of the backboard. Rule 1-8

Verbatim: “The restricted-area arc is a solid single-colored 2-inch line formed by a semicircle measured from the center of the basket to the inside edge with a radius of 4 feet and extending in a straight line to the front face of the backboard”.

title: Rules: NCAA men
text:
Transition defense

Transition take foul
A deliberate foul on the ball early in a break to stop the play before the numbers advantage can be used. Entry.
No such rule; checked against NCAA Men’s Basketball Rules Book.

The text was searched for the phrases take foul, transition, fast break and clear path; no transition-specific foul exists. The nearest provision is the flagrant 1 definition (Rule 4-15.2), which lists, verbatim, “Contact with an opponent that is not a legitimate attempt to play the ball or player”.

title: Rules: NCAA men
text:
Rules and regulations

Backcourt count
The time a team has to bring the ball across the midcourt line; the count a press is built to run out. Entry.
10 seconds. Rule 9-10

Verbatim: “shall not be in continuous control of a ball that is in the backcourt for 10 consecutive seconds”.



Court dimensions
The length and width of the playing court. Entry.
94 feet by 50 feet, inside the boundary lines. Rule 1-2.2

Verbatim: “The playing court shall be a rectangular surface free from obstructions with sidelines of 94 feet in length and end lines of 50 feet in length measured from the inside edges of these lines”.



Defensive three seconds
The NBA rule that a defender in the lane must be guarding someone within three seconds; the reason a rim protector cannot simply stand under the basket. Entry.
No such rule; checked against NCAA Men’s Basketball Rules Book.

The book’s three-second rule restricts the offensive player only; its text was searched for a defensive count and none appears. The offensive rule reads, verbatim: “it is a violation when a player exceeds three seconds in the lane and there is no try for goal”.



Free-throw lane
How wide the painted lane is; the number behind the paint, the blocks and the elbows. Entry.
12 feet, measured to the outside of the lane lines. Rule 1-6.1

Verbatim: “A free-throw lane, 12 feet wide measured to the outside of each lane boundary, and the semicircle with the free-throw line as a diameter, shall be marked at each end of”.



Free-throw line
How far the free-throw line is from the backboard; it fixes the nail and the elbows. Entry.
15 feet from the plane of the face of the backboard. Rule 1-6

Verbatim: “It shall be parallel to the end line and shall have its farthest edge 15 feet from the plane of the face of the backboard”.



Goaltending
Touching a shot on its way down, or off the backboard, while it can still score; the rule that limits what a rim protector may do. Entry.
A violation, alongside basket interference; only the defensive team’s goaltending awards points. Rule 9-15.1; Rule 5-1.18

Verbatim: “It is a violation to commit basket interference or goaltending” and “The only infractions for which points are awarded are goaltending or basket interference by the defensive team”.



Length of the game
How long a game is and how it is divided; the one rule every other clock hangs on. Entry.
Two halves of 20 minutes; extra periods of five minutes. Rule 5-6.1

Verbatim: “Playing time for varsity games shall consist of two halves of 20 minutes each with a halftime intermission of 15 minutes” and “Extra periods shall be five minutes each in length with a one-minute intermission before each”.



Shot clock
The time a team has to attempt a shot that reaches the ring; the number that sets the pace of every possession. Entry.
30 seconds. Rule 2-11.1

Under the duties of the shot-clock operator, verbatim: “Use a 30-second shot clock”.



Three-point line
How far the arc is from the basket, and how far the corner line is from the sideline; the geometry every spacing decision in Chapter 3 rests on. Entry.
22 feet 1¾ inches from the center of the basket; 21 feet 7⅞ inches in the corners. Rule 1-7.1

Verbatim: “The three-point field-goal line shall be a distance of 22 feet, 13/4 inches from the center of the basket to the outside edge of the three-point field-goal line and 21 feet, 77/8 inches in the corners”.

title: Special situations
text:
Inbounds, timeouts, presses and zone offense.
All families · 8 terms · 6 full, 0 partial, 2 short

ATO
Also: after timeout
A set play drawn up during a timeout, often the offense’s best-rehearsed action.

Why it is run. It is the one possession where all five attackers know the next four seconds and the defense has not seen this sequence today.
What beats it. Scouting, since a shape run twice in a season is guarded the second time; and switching, which takes the screens out of any script.
offense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also Set play


BLOB
Also: baseline out of bounds
An inbound play from under the offense’s own basket.

Why it is run. The inbounder sees all nine other players, the defenders near the rim must watch a ball behind them and a cutter in front, and five seconds is long enough for two screens.
What beats it. Switching every screen, hands up on the ball to shrink the angles, or a zone under the basket that guards the spots the cuts go to.
offense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also SLOB, Box set, Stack


Box set
An inbound alignment with four players in a square at the elbows and blocks.

offense · Special situations · short · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also BLOB, Stack


Press
Also: full-court press
Defensive pressure applied in the backcourt to force turnovers or slow the offense before it reaches the front court.

Why it is run. Pressure in the back court uses the sideline as a third defender and the count as a fourth, and against a team that cannot pass out of a trap it wins possessions faster than it gives up layups.
What beats it. The press break: the ball reversed away from the trap, the outlet to the middle, and the pass ahead to the player the safety cannot reach.
defense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 4.7 · See also Press break, Pick-up point


Press break
The offense’s set alignment and rules for advancing the ball against a press.

Why it is run. The middle of the floor cannot be trapped, because there is no line to trap against and the pass out has two directions; a press that fails has committed defenders behind the ball.
What beats it. Denying the inbounds pass rather than trapping after it, which attacks the five-second count; or taking the middle away first and steering the ball up a sideline.
offense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also Press


SLOB
Also: sideline out of bounds
An inbound play from the sideline in the front court.

Why it is run. A sideline entry is harder than a baseline one, so the play is built to get the ball in first, with a rim cut in front of it in case the defense sleeps.
What beats it. Denying the first pass to attack the five-second count, and switching the stack screens.
offense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also BLOB


Stack
An inbound alignment with four players in a line, who scatter on the slap of the ball.

offense · Special situations · short · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also BLOB, Box set


Zone offense
Offense built to attack areas rather than defenders, using the gaps between zone positions, the short corner and the high post.

Why it is run. A zone guards areas, so the answer is to overload a side, flash the soft spot where its rows meet, and skip the ball faster than the zone can shift.
What beats it. A match-up zone that closes out under control and picks up cutters; and the offense’s own impatience, since one pass short of the open shot is the usual failure.
offense · Special situations · full · Taught in lecture 3.12 · See also Zone defense, Dunker spot

title: Transition offense
text:
Scoring before the defense is set.
All families · 14 terms · 14 full, 0 partial, 0 short

Corner fill
Also: fill the corner, run to the corner
A lane runner continuing all the way to the corner rather than stopping on the wing.
Why it is run. The corner is the shot a retreating defense concedes last. Filling it also drags the low help defender away from the rim.
What beats it. A defender getting to the paint and then out to the corner, in that order.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Running the lanes, Corner, Low man


Fast break
Also: primary break
A transition attack that reaches the rim before the defense does, usually with a numbers advantage.
Why it is run. A layup or dunk against an unset defense is the best shot in the game. The break wins it by outrunning the defense rather than out-executing it.
What beats it. Getting the ball stopped and two defenders below the ball before the offense reaches the paint.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Numbers advantage, Outlet pass, Hit-ahead pass, Secondary break


Hit-ahead pass
Also: pitch ahead, kick ahead
A long pass up the floor to a player ahead of the ball, instead of dribbling it up.
Why it is run. The ball moves faster than any player runs. A hit-ahead skips the dribble and puts the ball in front of the retreating defense.
What beats it. The safety picking up the receiver early; pressure on the passer so the long pass is risky.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Push, Running the lanes, Outlet pass


Leak out
Also: cherry pick, cherry picking
A player leaving before the rebound is secured to get behind the defense.
Why it is run. One long pass can be a layup. The cost is a rebounder and a defender if the shot goes in or the rebound is lost.
What beats it. A defender staying with the leaker, and punishing the missing rebounder on the glass.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Hit-ahead pass, Floor balance


Numbers advantage
Also: 3-on-2, 2-on-1, odd-man rush
More attackers than defenders in the play, stated as attackers-on-defenders.

Why it is run. Each defender has to guard more than one player. The ball-handler forces one defender to commit, then passes to the player that defender left.
What beats it. Tandem defense, which puts the two defenders in a line so the front one takes the ball and the back one takes the first pass.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Fast break, Tandem defense


Outlet pass
Also: outlet
The first pass after a defensive rebound, from the rebounder to a guard on the wing or at the free-throw line extended.
Why it is run. The break starts on the outlet. A quick, clean outlet beats a defense that is still watching the rebound; a slow one lets them get back.
What beats it. Jamming the rebounder and denying the outlet man.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Fast break, Jam the rebounder, Push


Pace
The number of possessions a team plays per game; faster teams get more of them.
Why it is run. More possessions is more chances, and a team that thinks it is the better team wants more of them. Pace also shifts shots toward transition, where efficiency is highest.
What beats it. Slowing the game with the dribble, walking the ball up and using the shot clock.
offense / defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Push, Transition


Push
Also: push the ball, push the pace
Advancing the ball up the floor at speed, with the dribble or the pass, on every change of possession.
Why it is run. Pushing after a make as well as a miss forces the defense to sprint every possession. It compounds; the fourth-quarter legs are what the push is buying.
What beats it. Getting back on every make too, and picking up the ball early to slow the dribble.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Pace, Hit-ahead pass, Transition


Rim runner
Also: rim run
The big who sprints the middle of the floor straight to the rim ahead of the ball.
Why it is run. A big sprinting to the rim forces the first defender back to protect the paint, which means someone else is open, or the big is, for a seal and a lob.
What beats it. A defender back early enough to meet the big below the ball; the opposing big running with him.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Early seal, Trailer, Running the lanes


Running the lanes
Also: wide lanes, run wide
The wings sprinting up the sidelines, outside the ball, so the floor is wide when the ball arrives.

Why it is run. Wide lanes stretch the retreating defense sideline to sideline. A defender who sprints to the paint has left a shooter open on the wing or in the corner.
What beats it. Sprinting back to the paint first and closing out from the inside, taking the layup away before the three.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Corner fill, Rim runner, Hit-ahead pass


Secondary break
The scripted continuation when the primary break does not produce a shot, flowing into early offense without stopping.
Why it is run. The defense is back but not organized. The secondary break attacks that window with a quick action rather than resetting and letting them set up.
What beats it. Communicating the matchups fast, and having the rim protector home before the trailer arrives.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Fast break, Early offense, Drag screen


Trailer
The last player up the floor, usually a big, who arrives at the top after the first wave.

Why it is run. The defense has matched the first four; the trailer is the one nobody has. He can shoot, screen the ball as he arrives, or reverse the ball to the other side.
What beats it. The defender assigned to the trailer sprinting with him rather than settling in the paint.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Drag screen, Trailer flip, Rim runner


Transition
Also: transition offense, the break
The possession between a change of possession and the defense being set; the offense attacks before the defense can build its shape.

Why it is run. The defense has fewer players back, has not matched up, and has no rim protector in position. The offense is trying to score, or to draw a foul, before that changes.
What beats it. Sprinting back, stopping the ball early and protecting the rim first, before matching up.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Fast break, Secondary break, Early offense, Transition defense, Pace


Transition three
A three-point attempt taken in transition, before the defense has set, often by a trailer or a lane runner.
Why it is run. The defense sprints to the paint first, which leaves the arc open for a beat. A shooter who runs to a spot and stops gets that beat.
What beats it. Sprinting to the paint and then closing out under control; taking the layup away first is still the rule, so this shot is often a deliberate concession.
offense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 3.1 · See also Running the lanes, Trailer, Corner fill
